NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 Electronically Filed
 Intermediate Court of Appeals
 CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX
 30-OCT-2026
 08:09 AM
 Dkt. 102 SO
 NO. CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX

 IN THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS

 OF THE STATE OF HAWAI#I

 CLAUDIA ROHR, Plaintiff-Appellant, v.
 COUNTY OF HAWAI#I PLANNING DEPARTMENT; HUI HO#OLEIMALUO; and
 KA #UMEKE KA#EO PCS, Defendants-Appellees

 APPEAL FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE THIRD CIRCUIT
 (CIVIL NO. 3CCV-XX-XXXXXXX)

 SUMMARY DISPOSITION ORDER
 (By: Nakasone, Chief Judge, Leonard and Guidry, JJ.)
 Self-represented Plaintiff-Appellant Claudia Rohr

(Rohr) appeals from the April 1, 2024 Final Judgment (Judgment),

entered by the Circuit Court of the Third Circuit (Circuit

Court).1 Rohr also challenges the Circuit Court's March 3, 2023

Order Granting Defendant[-Appellee] County of Hawai#i Planning

Department's [(Planning Department's)] Motion to Dismiss

Complaint, Filed on November 18, 2022; March 3, 2023 Order

Granting Defendant[-Appellee] Hui Ho#oleimaluō's [(Hui's)] Motion

to Dismiss and Substantive Joinder in [the Planning Department's]

Motion to Dismiss Complaint, Filed November 21, 2022; March 3,

2023 Order Granting Defendant[-Appellee] Ka #Umeke K[ā]#eo PCS

 1
 The Honorable Henry T. Nakamoto presided.
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

(Charter School's) Substantive Joinder in [the Planning

Department's] Motion to Dismiss Complaint Filed on November 18,

2022 (collectively, the Dismissal Orders; the Planning

Department, the Hui, and the Charter School are collectively

referred to as Appellees); and March 4, 2024 Order Denying

[Rohr's] Motion to Reconsider or Amend [the Dismissal Orders]

(Order Denying Reconsideration).

 Rohr raises three points of error on appeal, contending

that the Circuit Court erred when it: (1) treated Appellees'

November 18, 21, and 22, 2022 Hawai#i Rules of Civil Procedure

(HRCP) Rule 12(b) motions (Motions to Dismiss) as tolling

motions; (2) dismissed the Amended Complaint under the doctrine

of primary jurisdiction; and (3) left Rohr unfairly disadvantaged

by the court's remedy.

 Upon careful review of the record and the briefs

submitted by the parties, and having given due consideration to

the arguments advanced and the issues raised, we resolve Rohr's
points of error as follows:

 (1) Rohr argues that the Circuit Court erred by

treating the Motions to Dismiss as "tolling" motions with respect

to Appellees' deadline to file an answer to the Amended

Complaint. In short, when the Circuit Court granted Rohr's

request to file an amended complaint, rather than requiring the

Appellees to file new – and likely substantially similar –

motions to dismiss the Amended Complaint, the Circuit Court

essentially kept Appellees' existing Motions to Dismiss pending

 2
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

as to Rohr's claims, and allowed them to supplement the Motions

to Dismiss, if necessary, to address the Amended Complaint.

 Rohr raised no objection to this procedure. It is

well-settled that issues not raised in the lower court will not

be considered on appeal. See, e.g., Kawamata Farms, Inc. v.

United Agri Prods., 86 Hawai#i 214, 248, 948 P.2d 1055, 1089

(1997). Accordingly, we conclude that Rohr's argument that the

Circuit Court abused its discretion in streamlining the pleadings

response process in this manner is waived.

 (2) Rohr argues that the Circuit Court erred in

applying the primary jurisdiction doctrine and dismissing the

Amended Complaint.

 Primary jurisdiction "comes into play whenever

enforcement of the claim requires the resolution of issues which,

under the regulatory scheme have been placed within the special

competence of an administrative body." Pac. Lightnet, Inc. v.

Time Warner Telecom, Inc., 131 Hawai#i 257, 268, 318 P.3d 97, 108
(2013) (cleaned up). While "conceptually analogous" to the

exhaustion of administrative remedies doctrine, the primary
jurisdiction doctrine "does not require a determination that the

court lacks jurisdiction over the matter." Id. at 268-69, 318

P.3d at 108-09 (citations omitted; emphasis in original).

"Instead, primary jurisdiction presumes that the claim at issue

is originally cognizable by both the court and the agency." Id.

at 269, 318 P.3d at 109 (emphasis in original) (citing Aged

Hawaiians v. Hawaiian Homes Comm'n, 78 Hawai#i 192, 202, 891 P.2d
279, 289 (1995)).

 3
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 Here, Rohr initiated proceedings at the agency level.

She petitioned the County of Hawai#i Board of Appeals (Board of

Appeals) on June 14, 2022, seeking reversal of the issuance of an

SMA Minor Permit to the Hui, arguing, inter alia, that the

challenged Kaumaui Project violated the General Plan, community

plan, and zoning, and therefore violated Hawaii Revised Statutes

(HRS) § 205A-26 (Supp. 2020).

 Less than three months later, before the Board of

Appeals had completed its decision-making, on September 6, 2022,

Rohr filed this suit in the Circuit Court, primarily arguing that

the SMA Minor Permit was approved without requiring the

preparation of an Environmental Assessment (EA) and, therefore,

was issued in violation of HRS chapter 343 (HEPA), Hawai#i

Administrative Rules (HAR) chapter 11-200.1, subchapter 9, and

article XI, section 9 of the Hawai#i Constitution. At that

point, the agency and the court proceedings took place alongside

one another. The Board of Appeals heard testimony concerning

Rohr's petition on September 9, and November 4, 2022. The Board

of Appeals Decision was issued on February 2, 2023. In light of

the Board of Appeals Decision, the Circuit Court orally stated at

the February 10, 2023 hearing on the Motions to Dismiss that Rohr

"can go through the proper procedures and appeal" via HRS § 91-

142 and that the court was dismissing this case without

prejudice.

 2
 Thereafter, Rohr did in fact timely file a notice of appeal from
the notice of Board of Appeals Decision.

 4
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 The primary jurisdiction doctrine applies here because,

pursuant to HRS § 343-7(a) (Supp. 2021), the circuit courts have

original jurisdiction over proceedings challenging the lack of an

EA required under HRS § 343-5 (Supp. 2021). See, e.g., Maui Lani

Neighbors, Inc. v. State, 156 Hawai#i 520, 542, 575 P.3d 610, 632

(2025).3 Under HRS § 343-7(a),4 a suit must be initiated within

120 days of the agency's decision to carry out or approve the

action, as Rohr did here, or within 120 days after the proposed

action is started if no formal determination was made. In

addition, an agency's action, including a determination not to

require an EA, is within the special competence of the

 3
 In Maui Lani Neighbors, the supreme court stated:

 HRS chapter 343 establishes a system of environmental
 review to ensure that environmental concerns are given
 appropriate consideration along with economic and technical
 considerations in decision-making processes. This allows
 for parties to challenge agency actions directly through the
 court system, as HRS § 343-7 explicitly contemplates a
 "judicial proceeding." Indeed, our courts frequently hear
 HEPA claims. See, e.g., Umberger v. Dep't of Land & Nat.
 Res., 140 Hawai#i 500, 403 P.3d 277 (2017); Kepo#o v. Kane,
 106 Hawai#i 270, 103 P.3d 939 (2005); [Citizens for Prot.
 of] N. Kohala [Coastline v. Cnty. of Hawai#i], 91 Hawai#i 94,
 979 P.2d 1120 [(1999)]. Clearly, the circuit court has
 jurisdiction to hear challenges brought pursuant to HRS
 § 343-7 given the plain language of the statute and
 extensive history of our courts hearing such cases.

 156 Hawai#i at 542, 575 P.3d at 632.

 4
 HRS § 343-7(a) provides:

 § 343-7 Limitation of actions. (a) Any judicial
 proceeding, the subject of which is the lack of assessment
 required under section 343-5, shall be initiated within one
 hundred twenty days of the agency's decision to carry out or
 approve the action, or, if a proposed action is undertaken
 without a formal determination by the agency that a
 statement is or is not required, a judicial proceeding shall
 be instituted within one hundred twenty days after the
 proposed action is started. The office, any agency
 responsible for approval of the action, or the applicant
 shall be adjudged an aggrieved party for the purposes of
 bringing judicial action under this subsection. Others, by
 environmental court action, may be adjudged aggrieved.

 5
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

administrative body issuing an SMA permit and may be challenged

through the appeals procedure set forth in HRS § 91-14, as

referenced by the Circuit Court. Thus, a HEPA claim is

originally cognizable by both the court and the agency and the

Circuit Court did not err in concluding that the primary

jurisdiction doctrine was applicable in this case.

 (3) Rohr further argues that, even if the Circuit

Court did not err in applying the primary jurisdiction doctrine,

she was unfairly disadvantaged by the court's remedy, i.e.,

dismissal of the case, as opposed to retaining jurisdiction and

staying the proceeding.

 This court has previously held:
 Where the doctrine of primary jurisdiction applies, the
 court has the "discretion either to retain jurisdiction [and
 stay the proceedings] or, if the parties would not be
 unfairly disadvantaged, to dismiss the case without
 prejudice." Reiter v. Cooper, 507 U.S. 258, 268–69, 113
 S.Ct. 1213, 1220, 122 L.Ed.2d 604 (U.S.N.C.1993).

Dancil v. Arakawa, 132 Hawai#i 472, 478, 323 P.3d 116, 122 (App.

2012).

 Rohr argues, inter alia, that "[a]ny judicial

proceeding, the subject of which is the lack of assessment
required under section 343-5, shall be initiated within one

hundred twenty days of the agency's decision to carry out or

approve the action;" however, that period "expired before the

Board of Appeals acted on Rohr's Petition for an appeal of the

Planning Director's decision to issue the SMA minor permit."

This argument has merit. The SMA Minor Permit was issued to the

Hui on June 6, 2022. Rohr petitioned the Board of Appeals on

June 14, 2022. The Board of Appeals Decision was not issued

until February 2, 2023. Had Rohr waited until the Board of

 6
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Appeals promulgated its decision, the statute of limitations for

her claims would have run pursuant to HRS § 343-7(a).

 The Planning Department argues that the running of a

statute of limitations is not per se an unfair disadvantage.

Both the Planning Department and the Hui argue that Rohr could

have raised the HEPA issue in her petition to the Board of

Appeals, but chose not to do so. Regarding the latter argument,

HRS § 343-7(a) expressly provides for a judicial action and the

Appellees provide no authority for the proposition that the

statutory right of action is foreclosed if the issue could have

been raised in an agency proceeding. Regarding the former

argument, under the circumstances of this case, we conclude that

Rohr was in fact disadvantaged by the dismissal of the Circuit

Court action "without prejudice," as prejudice effectively

attached when the case was dismissed because any newly filed suit

would be untimely under HRS § 343-7(a). See generally Fratinardo

v. Emps.' Ret. Sys. of State of Haw., 121 Hawai#i 462, 469, 220
P.3d 1043, 1050 (App. 2009) (noting federal cases finding that

the running of a statute of limitations constitutes a
disadvantage). Presumably, Appellees will at least argue that

HRS chapter 91 review of Rohr's HEPA challenge is waived in the

agency appeal because she did not raise it in her initial

petition to the Board of Appeals. Accordingly, we conclude that

the Circuit Court's dismissal, rather than the staying of Rohr'

NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 Electronically Filed
 Intermediate Court of Appeals
 CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX
 30-OCT-2026

 Dkt. 282 SO

 NO. CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX

 IN THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS

 OF THE STATE OF HAWAIʻI

 ASSOCIATION OF APARTMENT OWNERS OF KUHIO SHORES AT POIPU,
 Plaintiff-Appellee,
 v.
 WILLIAM H. GILLIAM, Defendant-Appellant, and
PACIFIC RIM PROPERTY SERVICE CORPORATION, A HAWAIʻI CORPORATION;
 Defendant/Counterclaim Plaintiff-Appellee, and DIRECTOR OF
 FINANCE, COUNTY OF KAUAʻI, Defendant-Appellee, and JOHN DOES 1-
10, JANE DOES, 1-10, DOE PARTNERSHIPS 1-10, DOE CORPORATIONS 1-
 10, DOE ENTITIES 1-10, AND DOE GOVERNMENTAL UNITS 1-10,
 Defendants.

 APPEAL FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE FIFTH CIRCUIT
 (CIVIL NO. 5CC161000063)

 SUMMARY DISPOSITION ORDER
 (By: Nakasone, Chief Judge, Wadsworth and Gluck, JJ.)
 Self-represented Defendant-Appellant William Gilliam
(Gilliam) appeals from the October 20, 2025 "Order Granting
Amended Receiver's Motion for Instructions Regarding Sale of
Property" (Order) and accompanying "Writ of Possession" (Writ)
issued by the Circuit Court of the Fifth Circuit (Circuit
Court). 1 Gilliam alleges that the Circuit Court improperly
granted the Order and Writ against him and

 1 The Honorable Randal G.B. Valenciano entered the Order and Writ.
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Defendant/Counterclaim Plaintiff-Appellee Pacific Rim Property
Service Corporation (PR1).
 Gilliam raises the following seven points of error on
appeal: 2 (1) "the [Circuit Court] lack[ed] jurisdiction by
service of process on any defendant"; (2) "the [Circuit Court]
lack[ed] subject matter jurisdiction [over] a claim to foreclose
a lien against a non-member"; (3) unclean hands; (4) "[an]
action for a receiver under [Hawai‘i Revised Statutes
(HRS)] § 414-422 is a special proceeding"; (5) "the court abused
its discretion by fail[ing] to stay pursuant to the special
motion to dismiss"; (6) "there is no issue preclusion"; and
(7) "the hearing on []September 23rd on the amended motion
improperly admitted hearsay [evidence] . . . and . . .
[disallowed] testimony [resulting in] a denial of due process."
 Upon careful review of the record and the briefs
submitted by the parties and having given due consideration to
the arguments advanced and the issues raised, we affirm.
 I. BACKGROUND
 At its core, this case is about ownership of a
condominium: Unit 209 of the Condominium Project, Kuhio Shores
at Poipu (Property). For many years, Gilliam has argued that he
owns the Property. He does not.
 In 2009, the Property was owned by PR1, a corporation.
Gilliam's mother, Vivian T. Lord (Lord), was the sole officer
and director of PR1. Lord passed away on June 6, 2009.

 2 Gilliam does not include a points of error section as required by
Hawaiʻi Rules of Appellate Procedure (HRAP) Rule 28(b)(4) (eff. 2022). As
such, his intended points of error and arguments are hard to discern. The
following points of error are taken from Gilliam's Opening Brief's section
headers. Where possible, we have tried to address each of Gilliam's numerous
arguments consistent with this court's "policy of affording litigants the
opportunity to have their cases heard on the merits, where possible." Morgan
v. Plan. Dep't, Cnty. of Kauai, 104 Hawaiʻi 173, 180-81, 86 P.3d 982, 989-90
(2004) (citation and internal quotation signals omitted).

 2
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 On April 28, 2016, the Association of Apartment Owners
of Kuhio Shores at Poipu (AOAO) filed a Complaint for
Foreclosure (Complaint) against PR1, Lord, and the Director of
Finance, County of Kaua‘i. The AOAO alleged PR1 and/or Lord were
the owner(s) of the Property and failed to pay various
assessments and fees.
 On April 27, 2017, Gilliam filed a Motion to Dismiss
the Complaint (2017 MTD), ostensibly on behalf of the
corporation that owned the Property ("Pacific Rim Property
Services Corporation"). 3 But "Pacific Rim Property Services
Corporation" (again, referred to herein as PR1) no longer
existed. Instead, Gilliam had incorporated a new entity with
the same name (referred to herein as PR2) with himself as its
sole officer and director.
 The AOAO filed a Memorandum in Opposition to the 2017
MTD, asserting that the Department of Commerce and Consumer
Affairs of the State of Hawai‘i records showed: (1) Lord was
PR1's sole officer and director; (2) Lord passed away on June 6,
2009; (3) PR1 was involuntarily dissolved on December 4, 2012;
and (4) Gilliam incorporated a new corporation with the same
name (again, PR2) on December 2, 2013, with Gilliam acting as
its sole officer and director. The AOAO asserted that it had no
information indicating that title of the Property had been
transferred from PR1. On August 15, 2017, the Circuit Court
granted in part and denied in part the 2017 MTD. 4

 3 From the record, it appears that Gilliam retained counsel to
represent PR1; however, Gilliam had (and has) no interest in PR1.

 4 The Circuit Court granted the motion as to attorneys' fees
imposed as a sanction against the AOAO for violating Rule 12 of the Rules of
the Circuit Courts of the State of Hawaiʻi.

 The Honorable Kathleen N.A. Watanabe entered the order granting
in part and denying in part the 2017 MTD.

 3
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 On June 26, 2018, the AOAO filed "Plaintiff [AOAO]'s
Motion for Appointment of Receiver" (Motion for Receiver). The
AOAO argued that PR1 was still the owner of the Property and
that a receiver was necessary to settle the unfinished business
of the corporation. Gilliam filed an opposition to the Motion
for Receiver — again, supposedly on behalf of PR1 — and argued
that he was a shareholder of PR1 at the time of Lord's death and
at the time of PR1's dissolution. Gilliam also claimed that he
inherited his mother's shares of PR1 upon her passing, such that
the Property had passed to him as the sole owner of the
corporation upon its dissolution.
 On October 19, 2018, the Circuit Court entered its
"Order Granting Plaintiff [AOAO]'s Motion for Appointment of
Receiver" (Order Appointing Receiver) and appointed George R.
Robinson (Robinson) as receiver for PR1. Robinson was tasked
with "assisting in all acts that are necessary for the final
settlement of the unfinished business of [PR1]" including
"determining the legal owner of the [Property]."
 On March 27, 2019, Robinson filed his Receiver Report.
Among other things, Robinson reported that Gilliam was "not
paying the real property taxes on the property and continuing to
rent the property out as a vacation rental." Robinson asked
that the Circuit Court approve his report, convert the matter to
a court-ordered sale of the Property, and grant him the
authority to complete the sale.
 On August 19, 2019, Gilliam filed for Chapter 11
bankruptcy — ostensibly on behalf of PR1. In re Pac. Rim Prop.
Serv. Corp., No. BAP HI-20-1071-BTL, 2020 WL 4371106, at *2
(B.A.P. 9th Cir. July 29, 2020). The Bankruptcy Court dismissed
the case. Id. at *2. The AOAO moved to annul the automatic
stay imposed by the bankruptcy proceeding, and the Bankruptcy
Court granted the motion. Id. Gilliam appealed the Bankruptcy

 4
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Court's annulment of the stay. Id. On appeal, the United
States Bankruptcy Appellate Panel of the Ninth Circuit held that
Gilliam did not have standing to challenge the annulment of the
stay. Id. at *3 (concluding that "Gilliam is not a shareholder,
much less the sole shareholder, of [PR1]" and that "[Gilliam]
has not identified any particularized or concrete injury arising
from the bankruptcy court's order annulling the stay of [PR1].
Gilliam is not [PR1], nor does he have any interest in or
control over [PR1] or its assets, including the [Property]").
 On October 2, 2019, the Circuit Court issued an "Order
Granting Plaintiff [AOAO]'s Motion for Instructions for the
Receiver" (2019 Order) and a "Writ of Possession" (2019 Writ)
for the Property. The 2019 Order directed the Receiver to sell
the Property to settle the debts of PR1. On November 1, 2019,
Gilliam appealed the 2019 Order and 2019 Writ.
 On October 25, 2019, Gilliam filed for Chapter 13
bankruptcy on behalf of himself, contending that the Property
was part of his bankruptcy estate. In re Gilliam, No. CV 20-
00194 JMS-WRP, 2020 WL 5848340, at *1 (D. Haw. Oct. 1, 2020),
aff'd, 859 F. App'x 832 (9th Cir. 2021). The Bankruptcy Court,
however, found that PR1 — not Gilliam — was the owner. Id. On
appeal, the United States District Court affirmed the Bankruptcy
Court's rulings and ruled that "[t]he Bankruptcy Court's factual
finding—that the condominium was not property of Gilliam's
estate—was not clearly erroneous, and is well-supported by ample
evidence in the record." Id. at *5.
 On April 17, 2024, this court ruled on the appeal of
the 2019 Order and 2019 Writ, vacating both and remanding for
further proceedings. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of Kuhio Shores
at Poipu v. Pac. Rim Prop. Serv. Corp., No. CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX,
2024 WL 1656266, at *2-3 (App. Apr. 17, 2024) (SDO). This court
concluded that although Gilliam was personally named in the 2019

 5
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Order and the 2019 Writ, Gilliam was never made a party to the
action (2024 Order). Id. at *2.
 On remand, on November 27, 2024, the AOAO filed its
First Amended Complaint for Foreclosure (FAC), adding Gilliam as
a defendant.
 On January 13, 2025, Gilliam filed a Motion to
Dismiss. The Circuit Court denied the motion. Gilliam then
filed various documents, including a Special Motion to Dismiss
(SMTD). The SMTD asserted that the FAC was a "SLAPP" action but
did not explain how or why, other than noting that the AOAO had
previously "slapped" the Property's common expense assessment
account with false entries. On March 12, 2025, the Circuit
Court denied the SMTD. 5
 Nine days later (on March 21, 2025), Robinson filed
"Receiver's Motion for Instructions Regarding Sale of Property"
and an "Amended Receiver's Motion for Instructions Regarding
Sale of Property" (Motion for Instructions). Gilliam filed an
"Opposition to Motion Writ of Possession & to Sell" (Opposition
to Motion for Instructions) arguing that the Circuit Court
should deny the Motion for Instructions. Gilliam then
unsuccessfully sought to remove the case to federal court,
delaying proceedings by several more months.
 On August 12, 2025, Gilliam filed an Answer and
Counterclaim to the FAC.
 On September 23, 2025, the Circuit Court held a
hearing on the Motion for Instructions and orally granted the
motion. This appeal followed.

 5 On March 28, 2025 — sixteen days after the Circuit Court had
ruled on the SMTD — Gilliam filed his Memorandum in Support of Special Motion
to Dismiss. This memorandum set forth arguments regarding the application of
HRS chapter 634G to his claim, among other things. The Circuit Court's March
12, 2025 order denying the SMTD did not address HRS chapter 634G, however,
because Gilliam had not raised the issue in his motion.

 6
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 II. DISCUSSION
 A. Ownership of the Property and Issue Preclusion
 At the outset, many of Gilliam's arguments are made on
behalf of PR1 or are based on his claimed ownership interest in
the Property. In Gilliam's sixth point of error, which we
address first, it appears that Gilliam argues the bankruptcy
decisions do not preclude him from claiming an interest in PR1
or the Property. He seems to argue that because one of the
bankruptcy cases was dismissed, and because this court
previously remanded this case, the Order Appointing Receiver has
been invalidated. Gilliam's arguments lack merit.
 First, the Order Appointing Receiver was not
invalidated by this court's previous ruling. This court vacated
the 2019

FOR IMMEDIATE NEWS RELEASE NEWS RELEASE #051

FROM: CLERK OF SUPREME COURT OF LOUISIANA

The Opinions handed down on the 30th day of October, 2026 are as follows:

BY Burris, J.:

 2026-C-00448 STEVE CROOKS, ET AL. VS. STATE OF LOUISIANA, THROUGH
 THE LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES, ET
 AL. (Parish of Rapides)

 APPELLATE COURT JUDGMENT AFFIRMED AS AMENDED.
 REMANNED. SEE OPINION.

 Weimer, C.J., dissents in part and assigns reasons.
  SUPREME COURT OF LOUISIANA

 No. 2026-C-00448

 STEVE CROOKS, ET AL.

 VS.

 STATE OF LOUISIANA, THROUGH THE LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT
 OF NATURAL RESOURCES, ET AL.

 On Writ of Certiorari to the Court of Appeal, Third Circuit, Parish of Rapides

BURRIS, J.

 In this class action, we reduce the attorney fee award to $16,713,656.20.

 FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

 The underlying facts of this case were set forth in Crooks v. Department of

Natural Resources, 19-0160 (La. 1/29/20), 340 So. 3d 574, opinion corrected on

reh’g (4/9/20) (“Crooks I”). As explained therein, in 1962, the United States began

constructing various structures in and around the Catahoula Basin to promote

navigation on the Ouachita and Black Rivers. Upon completion of the project, the

United States Fish and Wildlife Service began managing the water levels in and

around the Catahoula Basin. The State, through the Department of Wildlife and

Fisheries, also granted mineral leases in the area known as Catahoula Lake.

 In 2006, Steve Crooks and Era Lea Crooks filed a class action alleging they

represented a class of landowners in the Catahoula Basin whose property was

affected by increased water levels from the project. The trial court certified the

plaintiffs as one class, but subdivided the class into two groups, the Lake Plaintiffs

and the Swamp Plaintiffs, depending on the location of their properties. The Lake

Plaintiffs sought (1) ownership of the land between the ordinary low and ordinary

high water mark of the Little River located within the area known as Catahoula Lake;

(2) a declaration that these lands were unlawfully expropriated by the navigation

 1
 project; (3) damages for this inverse condemnation; and (4) recovery of the mineral

royalty and other payments received by the State from mineral leases granted over

the property. The Swamp Plaintiffs owned overflow lands located in the

southwestern portion of the Catahoula Basin. Because ownership of these

swampland tracts was not disputed, these plaintiffs sought only a declaration of

unlawful expropriation and damages for the inverse condemnation. See Crooks I,

340 So 3d at 577.

 The key issue presented to the trial court for the Lake Plaintiffs was the

classification of the area known as Catahoula Lake. The Lake Plaintiffs argued the

area was actually the banks of the Little River, thus conferring on the Lake Plaintiffs

ownership of the lands between the ordinary low and the ordinary high water mark.

La. Civ. Code art. 456 (“The banks of navigable rivers or streams are private things

that are subject to public use. The bank of a navigable river or stream is the land

lying between the ordinary low and the ordinary high stage of the water.”). The State

countered, arguing Catahoula Lake is a lake and the State owns the bed and waters

below the ordinary high water mark. La. Civ. Code art. 450 (“Public things that

belong to the state are such as running waters, the waters and bottoms of natural

navigable water bodies, the territorial sea, and the seashore.”). See Crooks I, 340 So.

3d at 577.

 Following a bench trial, the trial court rendered judgment in favor of the

plaintiffs, declaring the body of water in the Catahoula Basin in 1812 was a

permanent river that seasonally overflowed and covered its banks. Thus, the riparian

landowners, the Lake Plaintiffs, are the owners of these riverbanks. The trial court

also found the State liable for the inverse condemnation of these lands because of

the significant obstruction of the natural servitude of drainage. See Crooks I, 340 So.

3d at 578.

 2
  Specifically, the trial court declared the Lake Plaintiffs the owners of

22,813.48 acres of land and awarded them expropriation damages in the amount of

$28,745,438.40 based on $1,260.00 per acre, and $4,694,309.68 in oil and gas

royalties. The trial court also declared the Swamp Plaintiffs the owners of 7,580

acres of the overflow lands and awarded expropriation damages in the amount of

$9,550,800.00, based on the same value of $1,260.00 per acre. It further awarded

legal interest on all awards to run from May 4, 2006, until paid. The trial court set

attorney fees for class counsel in the amount of $22,075,843.82 and ordered seventy-

five percent of the attorney fee award to be paid by the State and twenty-five percent

to be assessed against the class common fund pursuant to La. R.S. 13:5111 and La.

Code Civ. Proc. art. 595. A judgment on all claims was signed on May 15, 2017.1

 On appeal, the appellate court found that since the taking of class plaintiffs’

land was committed by the United States, not the State, La. R.S. 13:5111 did not

apply. Thus, 100% of the attorney fees should be assessed against the common fund

pursuant to La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 597. The trial court’s judgment was affirmed in

1
 Regarding ownership of the land, this judgment stated:

 IT IS ORDERED, ADJUDGED, and DECREED that the body of water in the
 Catahoula Basin in 1812 was a permanent river that seasonally overflowed and
 covered its banks.

 IT IS FURTHER ORDERED, ADJUDGED, and DECREED that there be
 judgment herein recognizing that the class of plaintiffs identified as the riparian
 landowner plaintiffs (also known as the “Lake Plaintiffs”) are the legal owners of
 the river banks in the Catahoula Basin, consisting of 22,813.84 acres of lands
 located between the ordinary low water mark of the Little River and the ordinary
 high water mark of 36 feet mean sea level of the Little River, which lands are
 depicted in light blue and referred to as the bed and bottom of the so-called
 “Catahoula Lake” on the State’s exhibit introduced into evidence and identified as
 FW 202, a copy of which is attached hereto and made part of this final judgment.

 IT IS FURTHER ORDERED, ADJUDGED, and DECREED that there be
 judgment herein recognizing that the class of plaintiffs identified as the overflow
 landowner plaintiffs (also known as the “Swamp Plaintiffs”) are the legal owners
 of the 7,580 acres of land patented by the State of Louisiana in the southwestern
 portion of the Catahoula Basin, which lands are identified as property listing nos.
 29 through 83, and as the lands owned by W.H. Ward Properties, Inc., on the State’s
 exhibit introduced into evidence and identified as FW 202, a copy of which is
 attached hereto and made part of this final judgment.

 3
 all other respects. Crooks v. Department of Natural Resources, 17-0750 (La. App. 3

Cir. 12/28/18), 263 So. 3d 540.

 This court granted a writ of certiorari and found plaintiffs’ inverse

condemnation claims against the State for compensation had prescribed. See Crooks

I, 340 So. 3d at 584. Thus, the expropriation award of $28,745,438.40 to the Lake

Plaintiffs and $9,550,800.00 to the Swamp Plaintiffs was reversed. Id. at 587. In all

other respects, the appellate court judgment was affirmed. Id. Thereafter, this court

granted rehearing, solely for the purpose of correcting a footnote in the original

opinion to clarify that the award for attorney fees, expert witness fees, and costs was

not at issue in the writ application. Id. at 587 (on rehearing).

 After this court reversed the expropriation award, a disagreement arose

between class counsel and some members of the class regarding attorney fees. These

plaintiffs retained substitute counsel and filed a Motion to Set Attorneys’ Fees of

Class Counsel. These plaintiffs argued the attorney fees should be reduced

proportionally because of the reduction of the total award that occurred. The

plaintiffs argued that the common fund now only contained money from the royalties

awarded to the Lake Plaintiffs. Class counsel opposed, arguing res judicata barred

re-litigation of the 2017 attorney fee award. Class counsel also believed the common

fund consists of more than just the royalties awarded because it also includes the

future royalties and the value of the ownership rights secured over the land.

 The lower courts found the attorney fee issue had already been decided and

was res judicata. See Crooks v. Department of Natural Resources, 23-0478 (La. App.

3 Cir. 3/6/24) 2024 WL 954450 at *5. This court granted plaintiff’s writ application

and issued a per curiam directing the trial court to reconsider the award in light of

the significant reduction in the overall damages ultimately awarded to the class.

Crooks v. Department of Natural Resources, 24-0432 (La. 6/25/24), 386 So. 3d 1073

(“Crooks II”).

 4
  On December 6, 2024, the trial court held a hearing to reconsider the attorney

fees. The trial court used the Lodestar Method multiplying the total billable hours of

13,108.75 by an hourly rate of $425.00 per hour to reach an attorney fee award of

$5,571,218.75. Legal interest was also awarded from December 6, 2024 until paid.

 On appeal, the appellate court found the trial court abused its discretion when

it failed to apply a multiplier to the baseline lodestar fee. Crooks v. State Through

Louisiana Department of Natural Resources, 25-0478 (La. App. 3 Cir. 3/4/26), 433

So. 3d 21, 33. It multiplied the trial court’s award of $5,571,218.75 by a factor of

four to increase the attorney fee award to $22,284,875.00. Id. at 34. This is roughly

equivalent to the original attorney fee award, which was based on a one-third

percentage of the monetary award without considering the value of the property.

However, this is less than the original percentage method when factoring in the value

of the property and royalties. The appellate court considered that the evidence at trial

established the land is valued at $68,200,000.00 and that the royalty amount has

increased to approximately $9,000,000.00, for a total value of $77,200,000.00. Had

it not been for the efforts of class counsel over twenty years of litigation, the class

would not have $77,200,000.00 in land and royalties. Thus, it found the award of

$22,284,875.00 fair and reasonable. The appellate court also awarded interest from

the date of the first attorney fee award, May 15, 2017. Id. at 33-34

 Class plaintiffs applied to this court and we granted certiorari. Crooks v. State

through Louisiana Department of Natural Resources, 26-0448 (La. 6/25/26), --- So.

3d ---.

 DISCUSSION

 A court may award attorney fees in a class action when “as a result of the class

action a fund is made available, or a recovery or compromise is had which is

beneficial, to the class.” La. Code of Civ. Proc. art. 595(A). An appellate court

 5
 reviews an award of attorney fees for an abuse of discretion. Covington v. McNeese

State University, 12-2182 (La. 5/7/13), 118 So.3d 343, 348.

 Courts have relied on two methods to calculate class action fee awards, the

percentage of the fund approach and the lodestar approach. See Andrew J. Trask,

Fee Multipliers in Class Actions, 86 La. L. Rev. 405, 406 (2026). The percentage of

the fund approach calculates the fee based on the benefit the class receives. Id. The

lodestar approach calculates the fee by multiplying the reasonable amount of time

expended on the case by a reasonable hourly rate. Id. Here, the trial court used the

lodestar approach, multiplying the total billable hours of 13,108.75 by an hourly rate

of $425.00 per hour to reach an attorney fee award of $5,571,218.75. The appellate

court found the trial court abused its discretion when it failed to apply a multiplier

to the baseline lodestar calculation. Thus, it multiplied the trial court’s award by a

factor of four,

IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

In re: Appeal of Nyzinga Patterson : 
 : 
From Decision of : 
The City of Philadelphia : 
Fair Housing Commission : No. 513 C.D. 2024 
 : 
Appeal of: Nyzinga Patterson : Submitted: March 3, 2026 

BEFORE: HONORABLE LORI A. DUMAS, Judge 
 HONORABLE MATTHEW S. WOLF, Judge 
 HONORABLE MARY HANNAH LEAVITT, Senior Judge 

OPINION NOT REPORTED 

MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE WOLF FILED: October 30, 2026 

Nyzinga Patterson, (Tenant) an unrepresented litigant, appeals to this Court 
from an April 29, 2024 order of the Court of Common Pleas of Philadelphia County 
(trial court) denying her appeal from a prior order by the Philadelphia Housing 
Commission (Commission), which ordered Tenant to pay $7,200.00 in back rent to 
her former Landlords, Niraj Agarwal and Pearl Mathew (Landlords).1 Tenant 
contends that the trial court erred by finding that Landlords held a proper rental 
suitability certificate and by disregarding Tenant’s right as a tenant to a habitable 
dwelling. Because the trial court’s conclusions are supported by substantial 
evidence and legally sound, we affirm. 

1 Below, the trial court granted Landlords’ Praecipe to Intervene in the instant matter “given 
their standing as aggrieved parties.” Trial Ct. Op. at 6. 
2 
I. Background 
The following facts are not in dispute. In December 2019, Tenant signed a 
lease agreement with Landlords for a rental unit at 2107 East Lehigh Avenue in 
Philadelphia. Original Record (O.R.) at 10. Pursuant to the lease , Tenant made a 
payment of $42,881.61, which included $39,420.00 for 18 months of rent covering 
the period from January 1, 2020, to June 30, 2021; $1,271.00 in prorated rent for a 
portion of December 2019; and a $2,190.00 security deposit. Id. at 11. On April 12, 
2021, the parties agreed to renew their lease agreement for the period beginning on 
July 1, 2021, and ending on June 30, 2022. Id. Pursuant to a second lease renewal, 
signed by the parties on April 30, 2022, Tenant’s rent was increased from $2,190.00 
to $2,400.00 monthly, from July 1, 2022 , through June 30, 2023 . Id. Landlords 
received rent from Tenant through March 2023 but none for April, May, or June 
2023. Id. 
In March 2023, at Tenant’s request, Landlords sent her a copy of a Certificate 
of Rental Suitability (CRS) pursuant to Section 9-3903(1)(a) of the Philadelphia 
Code (Code).2 O.R. at 11. The effective dates of the CRS of which Tenant received 
a copy were March 13, 2023, to June 1 1, 2023. Id. Landlords then sent Tenant a 
nonrenewal notice on April 16, 2023, informing her that their lease agreement would 
not be renewed beyond the June 30, 2023 end of term. Id. On May 19, 2023, Tenant 
submitted a Fair Housing Complaint (Complaint) to the Commission; therein, she 
alleged that Landlords declined to renew the lease agreement in retaliation for her 
request that Landlords provide a rental license and banking data. Id. at 12. Tenant 

2 Section 9 -3903(1)(a) of the Code provides that the owner of any property rented for 
residential occupancy must provide tenants with a copy of the Certificate of Rental Suitability and 
of the City’s Good Housing Handbook “no more than sixty days prior to the inception of the 
tenancy.” Phila. Code § 9-3903(1)(a). 
3 
also contended that Landlords failed to furnish a lead certificate as required by Code 
Section 6-803(3).3 Id. at 11. While the matter was pending before the Commission, 
Tenant voluntarily vacated the property and relinquished possession to Landlords on 
June 30, 2023. Id. at 12. 
The Commission held a hearing on the matter on July 25, 2023. Id. at 45. At 
the hearing, Landlords, through counsel, argued that Tenant’s lease was not renewed 
because she was “habitually late in payments of rent” and “engaged in a verbally 
combative way with representatives of OCF [Realty] ,” Landlords’ property 
manager. Id. at 49. Landlords further argued that Tenant’s retaliation allegation was 
in any case moot, as she had already vacated the property on her own. Id. Tenant 
rejoined that Landlords were uncooperative in her efforts to ensure their compliance 
with the Code’s requirements of landlords. Id. 
In a July 31, 2023 final order, the Commission ruled that Tenant was to pay 
Landlords $7,200.00 in back rent by August 4, 2023. Id. at 13. The Commission 
explained that, while Landlords would be barred from recovery of back rent during 
the period when they did not hold a rental license, they came into compliance with 
that requirement on March 13, 2023; thus, the entire three -month period of 
nonpayment by Tenant (April, May, and June 2023) occurred at a time when 
Landlords were in compliance with the law. Id. As for Landlords, the Commission 
directed them to return Tenant’s $2,190.00 security deposit or a reduced amount 
accompanied by an itemized account of tenant damages. Id. The Commission 
further found that Landlords were not required to furnish Tenant with a lead 
certificate, as the rental property was built in 2018, well after the 1978 cutoff for the 

3 Section 6-803(3) of the Code requires all landlords leasing residential properties built before 
1978 to obtain a certification that the property is lead safe. Phila. Code § 6-803(3). 
4 
requirement. Id. Finally, the Commission dismissed as moot Tenant’s retaliation 
charge, given that she had already voluntarily vacated the property. Id. 
Tenant appealed to the trial court, which held its own hearing on April 29, 
2024. See Trial Ct. Tr. at 4. At the hearing, Tenant contended that the CRS which 
Landlords supplied in March 2023 was neither signed nor executed and therefore 
invalid. Id. at 11-12. Rejecting that contention, the trial court noted that a “[CRS] 
that has been dated and signed in March was submitted to the [C]ommission.” Id. 
at 13. 
In its April 29, 2024 order, the trial court denied Tenant’s appeal “due to lack 
of merit.” Tenant’s Br., App. 1, Trial Ct. Order. In an opinion provided to this Court 
pursuant to Pa.R.A.P. 1925(a), the trial court explains that Tenant’s “single claim 
referencing the unsigned copy of the CRS that had been initially submitted . . . did 
not comport with the Certified Record nor with [Tenant’s] sworn testimony before 
the Commission.” Trial Ct. Op. at 10 . The trial court notes that Tenant’s own 
Complaint to the Commission raised no signature issue but only acknowledged that 
Tenant was provided with copies of a rental license and a CRS in March 2023 . Id. 
at 11. “ Since all parties confirmed in multiple ways to the Commission that the 
required CRS had been provided to [Tenant] on March 13, 2023,” the trial court 
concludes that “the Commission had acted well within its discretion as factfinder.” 
Id. at 12. Because of Tenant’s “failure to present any convincing legal arguments or 
credible evidence to contradict the Commission’s findings,” the trial court maintains 
that it properly denied Tenant’s appeal. Id. at 13. This appeal followed.4 

4 The standard of this Court’s review where a trial court takes evidence de novo in an appeal 
from a local agency adjudication is to determine whether the trial court manifestly abused its 
discretion, committed error of law, or violated constitutional rights. McLaughlin v. Centre Cnty. 
Housing Auth., 616 A.2d 1073, 1074 n.3 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1992). 
5 
II. Discussion 
Section 9-3902(1)(a) of the Code provides that no person may offer for rent a 
one-family dwelling without first obtaining a housing inspection license from the 
Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I). Phila. Code § 9-3902(1)(a). Further, 
Section 9-3901(1)(e) provides that no person shall collect rent with respect to any 
property required to be licensed pursuant to the Code unless a valid license is issued 
for each property. Id. § 9 -3901(1)(e); see Philadelphia Code, PM –102.6.4. 
Reviewing courts have held that, while the latter provision bars a landlord from 
recovering unpaid rent while the landlord failed to comply, it “does not . . . provide 
the tenant with a legal right to require the landlord to disgorge any rents that the 
landlord had collected from the tenant during the period of noncompliance .” 
Ricchetti v. Ellis, (C.P. Phila., No. 130502703, filed September 7, 2016), aff’d (Pa. 
Super., 353 E.D.A. 2015, filed June 27, 2017). 
Instantly, the trial court found that Landlords were out of compliance from the 
beginning of Tenant’s tenancy until March 13, 2023, when they obtained a rental 
license from L&I effective on that date. Tenant paid rent for March 2023 but failed 
to do so for the last three months of her tenancy: April, May, and June 2023. Because 
Landlords were in compliance with Section 9-3902(1)(a) during that period, the trial 
court found that back rent was owed by Tenant to Landlord for those three months.5 
Accordingly, the trial court dismissed Tenant’s appeal of the Commission’s final 
order. 
On appeal to this Court, Tenant raises two issues for our disposition. First, 
Tenant maintains that Landlords’ signature was missing from the copy of the CRS 

5 It is not clear from the record whether Landlords—whose March 13, 2023 rental license was 
only effective until June 11, 2023—renewed their licensure for the last 20 days of Tenant’s term. 
Tenant does not contend that Landlords were out of compliance for that period, however. 
6 
that she received in March 2023; alternately, Tenant suggests that a signature was 
present but that it was “forged.” Tenant’s Br. at 6 (unpaginated). Tenant explains 
that the trial court’s failure to address the issue “undermines the integrity of the 
certification process and violates tenants’ rights to safe and habitable housing.” Id. 
Because Tenant “presented credible evidence” of Landlords’ noncompliance with 
Section 9 -3903(1)(a), she maintains that the trial court erred by dismissing her 
appeal. 
We disagree, as i t is not for Tenant to determine what evidence is credible; 
that function in this case was performed by the trial court. See McLaughlin v. Centre 
Cnty. Hous . Auth., 616 A.2d 1073, 1075 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1992) (explaining that , 
following a de novo hearing, “a trial court . . . must act as a nisi prius court” by 
weighing the evidence on its own). If Tenant had wished to contest the validity of 
Landlords’ CRS, whether because of an allegedly absent or forged signature, the 
time to do so was before the Commission. Thus, we see no reason to disturb the trial 
court’s finding that the CRS was valid as of March 13, 2023. 
Tenant’s second appeal argument is reproduced here in full: 

The decision conflicts with established law because it disregards the 
Philadelphia Code’s mandate that tenants are entitled to a habitable 
dwelling. The presence of habitability issues, which the court failed to 
address adequately, further undermines the v alidity of the landlord’s 
claims. 

Tenant’s Br. at 7 (unpaginated). 
It is well settled that this Court will decline to address arguments that a party 
has failed to develop. Goldata Comput. Servs., Inc. v. Dep’t of Banking and Sec. , 
350 A.3d 278, 298 n.26 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2025) (citing Pa.R.A.P. 2119). Here, Tenant’s 
brief states only the issue as recited above, but has no accompanying legal or factual 
7 
argument. Without more, this Court cannot engage in meaningful appellate review 
of the purported issue raised . Accordingly, Tenant’s second issue on appeal is 
waived. 
III. Conclusion 
Based on the reasons set forth above, we affirm the trial court. 

 _____________________________________ 
 MATTHEW S. WOLF, Judge 
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

In re: Appeal of Nyzinga Patterson : 
 : 
From Decision of : 
The City of Philadelphia : 
Fair Housing Commission : No. 513 C.D. 2024 
 : 
Appeal of: Nyzinga Patterson : 

O R D E R 

 AND NOW, this 30th day of October 2026, the order of the Court of 
Common Pleas of Philadelphia County in the above -captioned matter, dated April 
29, 2024, is hereby AFFIRMED.

SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-2520-24 

637 ARNOLD, LLC , 

 Plaintiff -Appellant, 

v. 

ARNOLD SHORES, LLC, 
HOLLSTON HILLS, LLC, 
HOLLSTON REALTY GROUP, 
LLC, BOROUGH OF POINT 
PLEASANT BEACH , and 
BOROUGH OF POINT 
PLEASANT BEACH ZONING 
BOARD OF ADJUSTMENT, 
jointly and severally , 

 Defendant s-Respondents. 
____________________________ 

Argued September 28, 2026 – Decided October 30, 2026 

Before Judges Sabatino and Torregrossa -O'Connor. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division, Ocean County, Docket No. L -2077-24. 

Ryan J. Murphy argued the cause for appellant (Gertner 
Murphy LLC, attorneys; Ryan J. Murphy , of counsel 
and on the brief s). 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-2520 -24 

John J. Jackson, III argued the cause for respondents 
Arnold Shores, LLC, Hollston Hills, LLC and Hollston 
Realty Group, LLC ( John J. Jackson III & Associates, 
Attorneys at Law , LLC, attorneys; John J. Jackson , III, 
of counsel and on the brief; Jilian McLeer, on the brief). 

Ben A. Montenegro argued the cause for respondent 
Borough of Point Pleasant Beach Zoning Board of 
Adjustment (Montenegro Thompson Montenegro & 
Genz, attorneys; Ben A. Montenegro and Ryan M. 
Amberger , on the brief ). 

PER CURIAM 
 This zoning appeal arises from site plan approvals and variance relief 
granted for renovation of the historic Gottlieb Building (the property ) located in 
the downtown commercial district of the Borough of Point Pleasant Beach (the 
Borough) . Specifically, t he Borough Zoning Board of Adjustment ( the Board) 
unanimously approved a project permitting mixed use of the two -story building 
and allowing construction of a restaurant and spa on the first level and a seven-
room hotel on the second floor (the project) . 
Plaintiff 637 Arnold, LLC , a neighboring property owner and objector to 
the project , sharing a common lot line with the property , now appeal s from the 
March 7, 2025 Law Division order dismissing with prejudice plaintiff's 
complaint in lieu of prerogative writs which it filed against the Board , the 
Borough, and the owners of the subject property, Arnold Shores, LLC, Hollston 

3 A-2520 -24 

Hills, LLC, and Hollston Realty Group, LLC (collectively Gottlieb defendants) ,1 
seeking reversal of the Board's approval . We have reviewed the record in light 
of applicable legal principles, and we affirm substantially for the detailed 
reasons stated by Judge Francis R. Hodgson , Jr., A.J.S.C., in his cogent oral 
decision accompanying the March 7 order, and his well-reasoned nineteen -page 
May 9, 2025 amplification of decision , provided pursuant to Rule 2:5-1(d). 
I. 
A. 
The following summary suffices to set forth the salient facts and 
procedural history pertinent to this appea l. Notably, t his was not the first zoning 
application approved by the Board to revitalize the Gottlieb Building, erected in 
1906 and located at 641 Arnold Avenue . In 2020 , prior to the Gottlieb 
defendants ' application , the property's previous owners sought , and in 2021 
obtained , variance relief to construct a first -floor marketplace and second -floor 

1 At all relevant times , defendants Arnold Shores, LLC, Hollston Hills, LLC, 
and Hollston Realty Group, LLC , acted jointly in furtherance of the application . 
Arnold Shores, LLC owns the property. "Business Entry Status Reports " for 
these entities contained in the record reflect that Arnold Shores, LLC's agent 
and principal is Hollston Hills, LLC. Don Slaght testified at the Board hearing, 
explaining he is the "principal [of] Hollston Hills, LLC, which is the managing 
member of Arnold Shores, LLC ." Thus, for clarity, we reference these 
defendants collectively as the Gottlieb defendants, the manner in which they 
were often jointly identified in the record and briefing. 

4 A-2520 -24 

hotel within the building , but never commenc ed the work. Plaintiff also 
unsuccessfu lly opposed th at earlier application. Here, the Gottlieb defendants 
sought variance relief pursuant to N.J.S.A. 40:55D -70(d)(1) and (2) and 
included new plans for the restaurant and spa . The proposed project retained in 
all respects the prior approved plan for the second -floor hotel . Thus, for context, 
we briefly review the 2020 application and approvals. 
The prior owners, then -represented by now-counsel for t he Gottlieb 
defendants , sought site plan approval and d(1) and bulk variances to "renovate 
and construct a[n] . . . addition to an existing commercial building" as well as 
"expand existing retail use and convert the upper levels to a hotel use on the 
property known as 641 Arnold Avenue." The prior application relied upon a 
January 23, 2019 survey of the land. The Board approved a d(1) variance, 
finding : the site to be "particularly suited" for the proposed use; the application 
met "the purposes of zoning . . . by promoting the public health, safety, morals, 
and general welfare"; "the proposed use w [ould] have no substantial negative 
impact on the surrounding property owners"; and "the relief sought d [id] not 
impair the intent and purpose of the Master Plan or Zoning Ordinance of the 
Borough." The resolution specifically granted d(1) variance approval for the 
hotel, which is not otherwise a permitted use in th at commercial zone. 

5 A-2520 -24 

As in the present matter , plaintiff then filed a n unsuccessful prerogative 
writs action in Superior Court seeking to reverse the Board's approval of the 
project . A prior judge upheld the Board's determination and dismissed the 
complaint. In 2023, the prior owners , having not moved forward with the 
approved project, sold the property to the Gottlieb defendants . 
Related to the 2020 application, Judge Hodgson , in an action addressing 
an apparent "boundary line dispute" pertaining to the property, "ordered the 
parties to proceed by commissioners pursuant to N.J.S.A. 2A:28 -1 et seq."2 The 
commissioners ' report corrected the property's common boundary line with 
plaintiff's property and included a new boundary line description and plat, but 
indicat ed they "[did] not attempt[] to determine if any of the structures on [the 
parties' lots] overlap the boundary line." On June 11, 2021, Judge Hodgson 
entered a "final order in th[e] matter" directing that "[t]he boundary line defined 

2 N.J.S.A. 2A:28 -1 directs: 

When any dispute arises between the owners of 
adjoining lands as to the location of any dividing line 
or lines between such lands, the Superior Court may, on 
application of either owner on notice to the other, 
appoint three disinterested commissioners, one of 
whom shall be a practical surveyor, who shall fix, 
ascertain and regulate such lines. 

6 A-2520 -24 

in the [c]ommissioner[s'] report shall be considered to have conclusively 
established the boundary line between the subject properties ." 
B. 
 In 2024, Arnold Shores filed its application for approval of a new 
integrated use of the property. It sought approval to retain the identical plan for 
the upstairs hotel, with a newly -proposed first-floor use to permit construction 
of a restaurant —a permitted use, and a spa—a non-permitted use . Public notice 
of the application followed , which advised : "Arnold Shores[,] LLC has applied 
to the [Board] for amended site plan approval and for any required use variance 
to allow the street level to be used as a restaurant in one section and a spa in 
another section where the second floor will be occupied by a p reviously 
approved non -conforming hotel use. " The notice included the date and location 
of the hearing, the specific address of the project, including lot and block 
number, and a description of the nature of the project . It disclosed that d(1) and 
d(2) "variances and[] design waivers" were sought, including use variances for 
the hotel and the spa, and also notified of the right to appear with questions or 
objections and the available means and manner to inspect the applica tion prior 
to the hearing. . 

7 A-2520 -24 

 The Board held three public hearings related to the application: March 7, 
2024; April 4, 2024; and May 30, 2024. Plaintiff appeared as an objector 
throughout the proceedings. The Board preliminarily addressed and rejected 
plaintiff's written and oral objections to the notice, and the Gottlieb defendants 
presented testimony over the various hearing dates from their manager, 
architect, licensed professional planner , and one of the owners . Over the course 
of the hearings, the Gottlieb defendants voluntarily submitted a revised site plan 
to both address certain concerns raised by neighbors and the Board about various 
aspects of the project and to reflect an updated survey incorporat ing the 2020 
correction of the boundary line with plaintiff's property. 
 At the conclusion of the testimony, the Board unanimously approved the 
application. On June 20, 2024, it issued a resolution memorializing the 
approval. After summarizing all the hearing evidence, the resolution expressly 
stated the Board found the Gottlieb defendants ' planner persuasive , and accepted 
and adopt ed the planner's testimony and conclusions concerning the project . 
The resolution , at time s citing directly to the planner's testimony, found the 
application: "met the requirements of N.J.S.A. 40:55D -70(d)(1) because the 
Board determined that the site is particularly suitable for this site " and "the 
proposed uses, . . . will be an attractive addition to the Arnold Avenue 

8 A-2520 -24 

downtown while providing vitality and convenience of multiple uses to area 
residents and visitors "; "the applicant has met the requirements of N.J.S.A. 
40:55D -70(d)(2) "; "the relief sought (with conditions imposed) can be granted 
without a substantial negative impact to the public good "; and "the relief sought 
(with conditions imposed) does not impair the intent and purpose of the Master 
Plan or Zoning Ordinance of the Borough of Point Pleasant Beach ." 
C. 
 On August 12, 2024, plaintiff filed its complaint in lieu of prerogative 
writs seeking reversal of the Board's approval. All defendants answered , and 
the Borough filed a motion to dismiss the complaint. Plaintiff moved to 
disqualify the Gottlieb defendants' counsel as a potential witness . The 
prerogative writ s trial was set for March 7, 2025. 
At the trial, plaintiff argued various alleged flaws in the zoning procedures 
and approvals necessitate d the court's reversing the Board. Summarized 
succinctly, plaintiff alleged : public notice was deficient because the description 
of the application failed to enumerate the correct variances required for the 
project ; the Board was required to , but did not , address the need for a d(1) 
variance for the integrated use of the property for restaurant, spa, and hotel, 
applied the incorrect legal standard, and improperly relied on prior approvals as 

9 A-2520 -24 

the multi -use project changed substantially from the 2020 plan for which 
approval was granted; the site plan was invalid as it relied upon an invalidated 
survey; the Board failed to consider public health and safety concerns related to 
building code violations ; the Board usurped the role of the governing body and 
permitted a new use by approving the "boutique hotel" without proper authority; 
and the Board and the Gottlieb defendants ' counsel were biased , tainting the 
proceedings . 
 Defendants countered that the notice was clear and adequate , and the 
amended site plan addressed any issues regarding the relatively insignificant 
changes to the boundary lines in the amended survey . They argued the Board 
properly addressed the requ

SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-0801-25 

LAKEVIEW REALTY 
INVESTMENT ASSOCIATES, LP, 

 Plaintiff -Appellant, 

v. 

CARLTON WILLIAMS -SEWELL 
and JOYCE PETERS , 

 Defendants -Respondents. 
______________________________ 

Submitted October 22, 2026 – Decided October 30, 2026 

Before Judges Chase and Augostini. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division , Camden County , Docket No. DC -009679 -25. 

Giordano, Halleran & Ciesla, P C, attorneys for 
appellant (Steven W. Ward , on the briefs). 

Carlton Williams -Sewell and Joyce Peters, self -
represented respondents. 

PER CURIAM 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-0801 -25 

Plaintiff Lakeview Realty Investment Associates, LP (Lakeview) appeals 
from a Special Civil Part order granting summary judgment to defendants 
Carlton Williams -Sewell and Joyce Peters. We vacate and remand . 
In February 2024, Lakeview filed a landlord -tenant complaint seeking 
possession of residential premises in Blackwood based on nonpayment of rent. 
On April 9, 2024, the parties entered into a consent agreement. The agreement 
provided in relevant part: 
1. The Tenant agrees to the immediate entry of 
Judgment for Possession and that the Warrant of 
Removal may issue and be served upon the Tenant at 
the Landlord 's request, as permitted by law, The 
Landlord agrees that the warrant of removal cannot be 
executed (no eviction) until [April 30, 2024] , ( "the 
move out date "), unless the Tenant fails to comply with 
[p]aragraph 2(b). 

2. The Tenant shall pay no money. Any possession 
remaining shall be considered abandoned. Defendant 
will return keys . 

3. a. If the Tenant does not make all payments required 
in [p]aragraph 2( [b]) of this Agreement , the Tenant 
agrees that the Landlord, with notice to the Tenant, can 
file a certification stating when and wha t the breach was 
and that that the warrant of removal can then be 
executed upon, as permitted by law , prior to the agreed 
upon move out date. [1] 

1 Paragraph 1 and paragraph 3(a) refer to "paragraph 2(b), " but the agreement 
contains no paragraph 2(b). This appears to be a drafting error . 

3 A-0801 -25 

That same day, the court entered a judgment for possession by consent. 
 On May 23, 2025, Lakeview filed this separate Special Civil Part action 
to recover unpaid rent that had accrued before the parties signed the consent 
agreement. Williams -Sewell responded by filing a copy of the consent 
agreement from the landlord -tenant matter. The court treated the filing as an 
answer and scheduled trial for September 2, 2025 . 
In August 2025, Lakeview moved for summary judgment, arguing 
defendants had filed no contesting answer. Lakeview also requested an 
adjournment of the trial pending disposition of that motion. The court denied 
the adjournment request. 
The parties appeared for trial on September 2, 2025. On the record, the 
court dismissed the complaint because it interpreted the consent agreement as 
waiving Lakeview 's right to recover any rent arrears from defendants. The court 
did not enter a written order that day. 
Ten days later, the court entered an order granting Lakeview 's motion for 
summary judgment. Around the same time, Lakeview moved for 
reconsideration of the court 's oral dismissal. A few days later, defendants 
moved to vacate the summary judgment order. 

4 A-0801 -25 

On October 15, 2025, the court entered an order denying Lakeview 's 
reconsideration motion. That same day, the court denied defendants ' motion to 
vacate the summary judgment order as moot. 
In November 2025, Lakeview filed a notice of appeal from the oral 
dismissal and the order denying reconsideration. The Appellate Clerk 's office 
informed Lakeview its appeal could not proceed because no written dismissal 
order had been entered. Lakeview then asked the trial court to issue one. On 
December 5, 2025, the court entered an order memorializing its earlier oral 
dismissal. 
 "A trial court 's interpretation of the law and the legal consequences that 
flow from established facts are not entitled to any special deference. " Rowe v. 
Bell & Gossett Co. , 239 N.J. 531, 552 (2019) (quoting Manalapan Realty, L.P. 
v. Twp. Comm. of Manalapan , 140 N.J. 366, 378 (1995)). The interpretation 
and construction of a settlem ent agreement is a matter of law for the trial court, 
subject to de novo review on appeal. Kaur v. Assured Lending Corp., 405 N.J. 
Super. 468, 474 (App. Div. 2009) (citing Spring Creek Holding Co. v. Shinnihon 
U.S.A. Co., 399 N.J. Super. 158, 190 (App. Div. 2008)) . 
 Lakeview argues the trial court misread the consent agreement. 
According to Lakeview, the agreement relieved defendants only of any 

5 A-0801 -25 

obligation to pay additional rent between April 9, 2024, and the agreed move -
out date of April 30, 2024. Lakeview contends the agreement did not waive its 
right to pursue unpaid rent accrued before April 9, 2024. 
Under our summary di spossess statute, landlords may elect an expedited 
procedure to regain possession of leased premises in the event of non-payment 
of rent. N.J.S.A. 2A:18 -53(b). But the Special Civil Part has limited jurisdiction 
in landlord -tenant cases . It adjudicates possession, not money damages . Hodges 
v. Sasil Corp. , 189 N.J. 210 , 221 (2007) (citing Hous. Auth. of Morristown v. 
Little, 135 N.J. 274, 28 0 (1994)). As the Court has explained, "[p]ossession of 
the premises is the only available remedy for non payment of rent, because 
money damages may not be awarded in a summary dispossess action. " Ibid. A 
landlord seeking unpaid rent therefore must file a separate action. 
Read in that context, the consent agreement did not waive Lakeview 's 
claim for rent arrears that predated the agreement. Paragraph 2 states "[t]he 
Tenant shall pay no money. " This means defendants did not have to pay 
additional money to remain in possession through the agreed move -out date. 
This language does not clearly release defendants from liability for rent already 
due under the lease before the parties signed the agreement. 

6 A-0801 -25 

The consent agreement reflects Lakeview did not require defendants to 
pay any money for allowing them to remain at the property from the three weeks 
between the consent agreement and the eviction date. And because the landlord -
tenant action could resolve only possession, not damages, Lakeview had no 
occasion in that proceeding to seek a money judgment for unpaid rent. Its failure 
to reserve expressly the right to bring a later collection action did not amount to 
a waiver of that right. 
The consideration recited in the agreement reinforces these conclusions . 
Lakeview agreed to delay execution of the warrant of removal until April 30, 
2024, and defendants, in turn, agreed to vacate and return the keys. The "no 
money" language addressed that brief post -agreement period of continued 
occupancy. Again, it did not extinguish liability for unpaid rent that had accrued 
earlier. 
Accordingly, the trial court was mistaken in construing the consent 
agreement as barring this action for unpaid rent. We therefore vacate the 
summary judgment order and remand for a trial on the merits. 
Vacated and remanded . We do not retain jurisdiction.

leads.caseName: Lampton Securities Partnership, LLP v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government
leads.text:
RENDERED: OCTOBER 30, 2026; 10:00 A.M.
 TO BE PUBLISHED

 Commonwealth of Kentucky
 Court of Appeals
 NO. 2025-CA-1380-MR

LAMPTON SECURITIES
PARTNERSHIP, LLP APPELLANT

 APPEAL FROM JEFFERSON CIRCUIT COURT
v. HONORABLE JESSICA E. GREEN, JUDGE
 ACTION NO. 20-CI-003017

LOUISVILLE-JEFFERSON COUNTY
METRO GOVERNMENT AND
METROPOLITAN SEWER DISTRICT APPELLEES

 OPINION
 AFFIRMING

 ** ** ** ** **

BEFORE: COMBS, EASTON, AND L. JONES, JUDGES.

JONES, L., JUDGE: Lampton Securities Partnership (Lampton) appeals from the

Jefferson Circuit Court’s order granting summary judgment to Louisville-Jefferson

County Metro Government (Metro Government) and the Metropolitan Sewer

District (Metro Sewer) in this reverse condemnation action. We affirm.
  In the early 1990s, the owners of a roughly four-acre tract along the

Ohio River received approval from Metro Sewer to construct condominiums. The

plan approved by Metro Sewer contained two phases of construction.1 Though it is

uncontested that the owners received approval of the plan, the actual permit is not

in the record. Phase One was completed on roughly two acres. The remaining two

1
 Metro Government and Metro Sewer seem to dispute both phases were approved. But the
deposition testimony of Metro Sewer’s designated representative indicates that both were
approved:

 Q. Okay. So [Metro Sewer] approved the construction plans—

 A. Yeah, that was back in ’92.

 Q. Back in ’92. Okay. And do you recall what those plans
 entailed?

 A. They showed a condo, a large condo complex. It had a Phase 1
 and a Phase 2. Phase 1 was the only one that was built.

 Q. Right. But both phases were approved.

 A. They were both shown on the plan.

 Q. They were both shown on the plan.

 A. (Nods head affirmatively)

 Q. It was a total of four acres, and that was the development that
 was approved by [Metro Sewer] in 1992 or ’93, correct?

 A. ’92, yes.

 Q. In ’92. So there is no question that [Metro Sewer] approved
 the development of both tracts of land in 1992, correct?

 A. It appeared to be a single tract on the plans that we have.

Trial Court Record (TR) at 628.

 -2-
 acres (Tract) were the planned location for Phase Two. A building to house

electrical equipment was erected on the Tract, and utility lines were put in place.

However, no condominiums were built on the Tract.

 Meanwhile, in 1997, the Metro Government enacted floodplain

ordinances in response to catastrophic flooding. Essentially, the ordinances

prevent most types of new construction on land within the “conveyance zone”

portion of the floodplain. The Tract is within the conveyance zone.

 However, the ordinances have two relevant exceptions. First, they

permit the continuation of construction which had already begun before the

ordinances were adopted. Second, an impacted landowner is permitted to seek a

variance from Metro Sewer’s Floodplain Board (Board).2 The record contains

evidence of variances the Board has granted to other landowners.

2
 In relevant part, § 157.03(A)(1) provides that “[n]o development . . . shall occur in the local
regulatory conveyance zone except as approved in a permit issued by the administering agency”
but subsection (C)(8) allows the continuation of a nonconforming use “which was lawful on the
effective date of this chapter . . . .” Ordinance § 157.04(B) provides that the Board “may grant”
a “specific variance from the individual provisions of § 157.03 . . . .”

 Metro Government’s official website contains a hyperlink leading to the American Legal
Publishing Company’s website, where the entirety of local ordinances and code provisions may
be viewed. See https://louisvilleky.gov/government/codes-regulations/local-ordinances (last
visited Oct. 2, 2026). The ordinances quoted above thus may be viewed at
https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/louisvillemetro/latest/loukymetro/0-0-0-
17164#JD_157.03 (last visited Oct. 2, 2026). We used the same method to view another
municipality’s ordinances in Schell v. Young, 640 S.W.3d 24, 30 n.2 (Ky. App. 2021).

 -3-
  In 1998, after the enactment of the floodplain ordinances, Lampton

purchased the Tract for $800,000.00. The Tract sat idle until Lampton placed it on

the market around 2019. The marketing materials asserted that the Tract could be

commercially developed. Metro Sewer personnel somehow learned the Tract was

for sale and a meeting eventually occurred between Metro Sewer’s counsel and

Lampton. At that meeting, Metro Sewer’s counsel opined that the floodplain

ordinances prevented development of the Tract.

 Lampton neither sought a variance nor attempted to begin the

construction of Phase Two (in reliance upon the previously granted permit).

Instead, in May 2020, Lampton filed this reverse condemnation action against

Metro Sewer and Metro Government. The complaint asserts Lampton “lost all

economically beneficial uses” of the Tract because of the enactment and

enforcement of the floodplain ordinances. TR at 9.

 After protracted discovery and vigorous motion practice, the trial

court granted summary judgment to Metro Sewer and Metro Government in July

2025. Though the parties had raised additional arguments, the trial court’s

decision was based on two conclusions. First, the court concluded that Lampton

had failed to exhaust its administrative remedies. Second, the court concluded the

complaint had not been timely filed. After the court denied its motion to alter,

amend, or vacate, Lampton filed this appeal.

 -4-
  Kentucky’s familiar summary judgment standards are:

 In considering a motion for summary judgment, a
 trial court must view the record in a light most favorable
 to the non-moving party, resolving all doubts in its favor.
 Steelvest, Inc. v. Scansteel Serv. Ctr., Inc., 807 S.W.2d
 476, 480 (Ky. 1991). The trial court may grant summary
 judgment only if it concludes that no disputed issues of
 material fact exist for trial. Id. On appeal of a summary
 judgment, we must determine whether the trial court
 correctly found that the moving party was entitled to a
 judgment as a matter of law. Id. Because summary
 judgment involves questions of law, we need not defer to
 the trial court’s conclusions; accordingly, we review the
 record de novo. Blevins v. Moran, 12 S.W.3d 698, 700-
 01 (Ky. App. 2000).

Waugh v. Parker, 584 S.W.3d 748, 750–51 (Ky. 2019).

 Of course, under settled Kentucky precedent, “[i]f an appellate court

is aware of a reason to affirm the lower court’s decision, it must do so, even if on

different grounds.” Mark D. Dean, P.S.C. v. Commonwealth Bank & Tr. Co., 434

S.W.3d 489, 496 (Ky. 2014) (emphasis added). Pursuant to that principle, after

examining the record and applicable law, we conclude that Metro Sewer and Metro

Government are entitled to summary judgment because Lampton’s claims are not

ripe.

 Under §§ 13 and 242 of the Kentucky Constitution and the Fifth

Amendment to the United States Constitution, “the government may not take a

citizen’s private property without providing just compensation.” Farmers Nat’l

Bank v. Commonwealth Dep’t of Revenue, 486 S.W.3d 872, 883 (Ky. App. 2015).

 -5-
 The classic version of a taking occurs when the government seizes property for its

own use. See, e.g., Palazzolo v. Rhode Island, 533 U.S. 606, 617 (2001) (“The

clearest sort of taking occurs when the government encroaches upon or occupies

private land for its own proposed use.”).

 However, there is another type of governmental taking variously

referred to as a reverse taking, an inverse taking, an inverse condemnation, or a

regulatory taking. “Inverse condemnation is the term applied to a suit against a

government to recover the fair market value of property which has in effect been

taken and appropriated by the activities of the government when no eminent

domain proceedings are used.” Commonwealth, Nat. Res. and Env’t Prot. Cabinet

v. Stearns Coal and Lumber Co., 678 S.W.2d 378, 381 (Ky. 1984). As the United

States Supreme Court has described it, “there will be instances when government

actions do not encroach upon or occupy the property yet still affect and limit its use

to such an extent that a taking occurs” because the applicable governmental

regulation “goes too far. . . .” Palazzolo, 533 U.S. at 617 (internal quotation marks

and citations omitted). A governmental regulation “goes too far” when it “denies

all economically beneficial or productive use of land. . . .” Id. (internal quotation

marks and citations omitted). That is what Lampton asserts occurred here.

 But “[a] court cannot determine whether a regulation has gone ‘too

far’ unless it knows how far the regulation goes.” MacDonald, Sommer & Frates

 -6-
 v. Yolo Cnty., 477 U.S. 340, 348 (1986). Thus, as the Supreme Court has

explained:

 a takings claim based on a law or regulation which is
 alleged to go too far in burdening property depends upon
 the landowner’s first having followed reasonable and
 necessary steps to allow regulatory agencies to exercise
 their full discretion in considering development plans for
 the property, including the opportunity to grant any
 variances or waivers allowed by law. As a general rule,
 until these ordinary processes have been followed the
 extent of the restriction on property is not known and a
 regulatory taking has not yet been established.

Palazzolo, 533 U.S. at 620–21. The Supreme Court further stated that “[u]ntil a

property owner has obtained a final decision regarding the application of the

zoning ordinance and subdivision regulations to its property, it is impossible to tell

whether the land retain[s] any reasonable beneficial use or whether [existing]

expectation interests ha[ve] been destroyed.” Yolo County, 477 U.S. at 349.

(internal quotation marks and citations omitted).

 The Supreme Court has explained that a case is not ripe until a “final

decision” has been made because the entities who enforce local land-use policies

possess a “high degree of discretion” to grant exceptions to those policies, so “a

sound judgment about what use will be allowed simply cannot be made by asking

whether a parcel’s characteristics or a proposal’s details facially conform to the

terms of the general use regulations.” Suitum v. Tahoe Reg’l Plan. Agency, 520

U.S. 725, 739 (1997). In plain English, a takings claim is not ripe “if avenues still

 -7-
 remain for the government to clarify or change its decision.” Pakdel v. City and

Cnty. of San Francisco, California, 594 U.S. 474, 480 (2021).

 Although those Supreme Court decisions were based on federal law

and the United States Constitution, the same general ripeness principles apply

under Kentucky law. For example, our Supreme Court applied ripeness principles

to a reverse condemnation claim brought under Kentucky law in Spanish Cove

Sanitation, Inc. v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District, 72

S.W.3d 918 (Ky. 2002). In Spanish Cove Sanitation, the owner of a wastewater

treatment facility filed a reverse condemnation action when Metro Sewer had

merely “planned to tie into the pipe system that served [the wastewater treatment

facility’s] customers.” Id. at 919. In other words, the plaintiff filed suit based on

only a plan, without Metro Sewer having actually “tied into” the plaintiff’s sewer

lines. Id.

 Our Supreme Court held the suit was not ripe:

 At the outset, we should note that the trial court
 did not abuse its discretion in determining that the issue
 was not ripe. Under Kentucky law, before a plaintiff can
 make a claim of inverse condemnation, there must be an
 actual taking. Holloway Const. Co. v. Smith, Ky., 683
 S.W.2d 248, 249 (1984). In Associated Industries of
 Kentucky v. Commonwealth, Ky., 912 S.W.2d 947
 (1995), we held that Kentucky courts cannot grant
 advisory opinions or rule on hypothetical questions, but
 rather must rule on real disputes. At the time this action
 was filed, nothing had even arguably been taken.

THE CRYSTAL BEACH CONDOMINIUM ASSOCIATION, INC., an Idaho Non-Profit Corporation; MARVIN ASKEY, ROBERT SCHWENKFELDER, EDWARD BARRETT, CHRISTOPHER BRAZIL, RONALD GROVE, MICHAEL VIRDEN, MARY MARTIN, PATTI ZATICA, TYLER BUTTERFIELD, DARRELL CARNEY, JOHN DOES 1-60 AND JANE DOES 1-60, Encroachers
