When an applicant seeks to amend a property's zoning designation to an EEO district in furtherance of an adaptive reuse development project, the applicant must submit a rezoning application to the Town Board along with a conceptual development plan specifying certain information about the project proposal and the existing conditions of the property, among other things ( see Code of the Town of Rochester § 140-18.1 [A] [3]; [B] [2] [c], [f]). The Town Board then reviews the application and may either reject it or hold a public hearing on the matter ( see Code of the Town of Rochester § 140-18.1 [C] [2]). Following a public hearing, "the Town Board may, in its sole legislative discretion, act to approve, approve with modification[s] or conditions, or disapprove the rezoning application" (Code of the Town of Rochester § 140-18.1 [C] [7]). 
 As for the Planning

leads.caseName: Seneca Ins. Co. Inc. v. Cobleskill Enter., LLP
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Seneca Ins. Co. Inc. v Cobleskill Enter., LLP 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06366 
 October 29, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Third Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Seneca Insurance Company Inc., Appellant- Respondent, 
 v 
 Cobleskill Enterprise, LLP, Defendant, and Links Insurance Services, LLC, Respondent- Appellant. 

 Decided and Entered:October 29, 2026 
 CV-25-0548 
 Calendar Date: September 9, 2026 
 Before: Garry, P.J., Aarons, Pritzker, Mcshan And Mackey, JJ. 

 Maguire Tedrick, PLLC, Wantagh (Katherine Maguire Tedrick of counsel), for appellant-respondent. 
 Kaufman Dolowich LLP, White Plains (Howard S. Kronberg of counsel), for respondent-appellant. 

 [*1] 
 Pritzker, J. 
 Cross-appeals from an order of the Supreme Court (James Ferreira, J.), entered March 4, 2025 in Schoharie County, which denied a motion by defendant Links Insurance Services, LLC to dismiss the complaint against it and denied plaintiff's cross-motion for summary judgment. 
 In 2018, following a fire at its hotel and restaurant complex in the Town of Cobleskill, Schoharie County, defendant Cobleskill Enterprise, LLP (hereinafter defendant) attempted to file a claim for coverage under its commercial property insurance policy. Plaintiff, defendant's insurer, denied the claim on various grounds, including misrepresentations in the policy application as well as in the claim and defendant's breach of the policy's protective safeguards endorsement (hereinafter PSE). When defendant continued to seek coverage for the fire, plaintiff commenced this action for fraud and for declarations that the policy was void and that it did not have to provide coverage for the fire. Defendant joined issue, counterclaimed for breach of the policy and then commenced a third-party action against defendant Links Insurance Services, LLC, the retail broker it worked with to obtain its policy. Defendant asserted that, in the event Supreme Court concluded that plaintiff was not required to cover the fire because the policy had been cancelled due to nonpayment or that the policy was void due to misrepresentations made during the application process, such outcomes would be the result of various breaches of duty and/or negligence by Links; as such, defendant would be entitled to the full amount from Links that it would have received under the policy had it covered the fire and any further expenses it had incurred in reliance on Links' representations. Links joined issue. 
 Plaintiff thereafter amended the complaint to assert direct claims against Links for fraud and negligent misrepresentation, asserting that Links had filed defendant's claim for coverage of the fire despite knowledge that the policy had actually been cancelled by a third party before the fire occurred. Following joinder of issue on the amended complaint, Links moved to dismiss all claims asserted against it by plaintiff and defendant pursuant to CPLR 3211 (a) (7), and plaintiff cross-moved for summary judgment against defendant declaring that it was not obligated to cover the fire based upon, among other things, plaintiff's failure to maintain smoke detectors in violation of the policy's PSE. During the pendency of the motions, defendant amended its claims to add new allegations of breach of duty by Links, and Links filed an "amended" motion seeking dismissal of same. Supreme Court denied both motions, concluding, as relevant here, that plaintiff had stated claims against Links for fraud and negligent misrepresentation, and that defendant had stated claims against Links for negligence and breach of duty. The court also concluded that plaintiff's own submissions raised triable issues of fact as to whether defendant breached [*2] the PSE, and thus it failed to satisfy its prima facie burden on its cross-motion for summary judgment against defendant. Plaintiff and Links cross-appeal. 
 First, we turn to plaintiff's assertion that Supreme Court erred in denying its cross-motion for summary judgment against defendant. Specifically, plaintiff contends that it was not obligated to cover the fire because defendant breached the policy's PSE, as asserted in plaintiff's sixth cause of action in its August 2023 amended complaint. "[S]ummary judgment can only be granted if the movant tenders sufficient evidence to demonstrate the absence of any material issues of fact and, once this prima facie showing is made, the non-movant fails to produce evidentiary proof in admissible form sufficient to establish the existence of material issues of fact which require a trial of the action" ( Maloney v Night Castle Mgt. , 249 AD3d 1260, 1261 [3d Dept 2026] [internal quotation marks and citations omitted]). As relevant here, "[u]nder New York law, insurance contracts are construed by applying general principles of contract interpretation," and, consequently, "[u]nambiguous provisions . . . must be given their plain and ordinary meaning," with their interpretation posing "a question of law for the court" ( Consolidated Rest. Operations, Inc. v Westport Ins. Corp. , 41 NY3d 415, 426 [2024] [internal quotation marks and citations omitted]; see Burlington Ins. Co. v NYC Tr. Auth. , 29 NY3d 313, 321 [2017]). As also relevant here, Insurance Law § 3106 provides that a warranty "means any provision of an insurance contract which has the effect of requiring, as a condition precedent of the taking effect of such contract or as a condition precedent of the insurer's liability thereunder, the existence of a fact which tends to diminish, or the non-existence of a fact which tends to increase, the risk of the occurrence of any loss, damage, or injury within the coverage of the contract" (Insurance Law § 3106 [a]). "A breach of a warranty shall not avoid an insurance contract or defeat recovery thereunder unless such breach materially increases the risk of loss, damage or injury within the coverage of the contract" (Insurance Law § 3106 [b]). It is the burden of the insurer to establish that the warranty was breached and that such breach was material, with materiality generally constituting a question of fact unless the evidence thereof is "clear and substantially uncontradicted" ( Anjay Corp. v Those Certain Underwriters at Lloyd's of London Subscribing to Certificate No. HN01AAF4393 , 33 AD3d 323, 324 [1st Dept 2006] [internal quotation marks and citations omitted]; see e.g. 730 J & J v Twin City Fire Ins. Co. , 293 AD2d 519, 520 [2d Dept 2002]). 
 At the outset, it is not disputed that the PSE constitutes a warranty, and indeed explicitly requires as a "condition" of coverage that the property maintain operational smoke detectors in its units and common areas, a fact which would logically reduce the covered risk of [*3] loss from fire ( see Insurance Law § 3106 [a]; Anghel v Utica Mut. Ins. Co. , 127 AD3d 897, 899 [2d Dept 2015]; see also Triple Diamond CafÉ, Inc. v Those Certain Underwriters at Lloyd's London , 124 AD3d 763, 765 [2d Dept 2015]; J.A.V. Petroleum Inc. v Norguard Ins. Co. , 2018 WL 10676901, *6, 2018 US Dist LEXIS 236209, *16-17 [ED NY, June 19, 2018, No. 17-CV-5107(SJF)(ARL)]). Thus, the issue distills to whether plaintiff established that there are no material issues of fact and thus that defendant, as a matter of law, breached the PSE and that such breach materially increased the risk of loss under the policy ( see Insurance Law § 3106 [b]). 
 In support of its cross-motion, plaintiff offered a copy of defendant's insurance policy. In the attached PSE, the policy provides that, "[a]s a condition of this insurance, [defendant is] required to maintain" certain protective safeguards, which includes "either operational hard wired or operational battery powered smoke detectors in each unit and common areas" of the premises. The PSE added that plaintiff would "not pay for loss or damage caused by or resulting from fire . . . if, prior to the fire," defendant either "[k]new of any suspension or impairment in any protective safeguard . . . and failed to notify [plaintiff] of that fact" or "[f]ailed to maintain any protective safeguard . . . over which [defendant] had control, in complete working order." Plaintiff also offered documentation showing that defendant had been cited by the Village of Cobleskill in October 2018 for failing to maintain appropriate carbon monoxide detectors and an agreement between defendant and a fire equipment firm signed roughly one month later to "upgrade[ ] and add[ ]" fire alarm system devices "throughout the building." 
 Plaintiff further submitted the deposition testimony of a technician from the fire equipment firm who explained that, in mid-November 2018, defendant asked his firm to "take a look" at the property's fire alarm system because the Village's "code department was on them" to install carbon monoxide detectors and tie them into the property's fire alarm system. When he inspected the property's fire alarm system, he discovered that it relied on "older detectors," incorporated two different, incompatible types of systems, and could not be modified to incorporate carbon monoxide detectors. As a result, he concluded that "the entire system" needed to be replaced. The technician testified that there were no smoke detectors in the pool area, bowling alley, basement or in the ceiling area of the dining room. Further, although the property's banquet room had heat detectors, it did not have smoke detectors. Similarly, there were only heat detectors, not smoke detectors, in the kitchen. The technician explained that he considered the property's common areas to encompass areas like the pool, hallways and the lobby, as well as areas like the dining room and banquet room if they were open to the public. The technician testified [*4] that the firm was hired to bring defendant's premises into compliance, which included, among other things, installation of a new, unified fire alarm panel, 124 new smoke detectors throughout the property and new, fireproof wiring for the property's detectors. During his work, he discovered that a few smoke detectors in the hallway between the restaurant's kitchen and dining room and "by the pool area" were nonfunctional "dummy detectors." He also discovered that the reporting panel for the restaurant, kitchen, banquet room, bowling alley and some of the property's offices was unable to communicate with the main fire alarm panel in the hotel's lobby, and thus a fire in those areas would not set off the building's fire alarms. The technician recalled that work paused on December 19, 2018, and he learned that there had been a fire on the premises a few days later, on December 24, 2018. Upon inspecting the premises after the fire, he saw smoke damage throughout the premises and extensive burn damage in the property's basement. 
 Here, plaintiff successfully established both that there were no material issues of fact inasmuch as defendant breached the PSE and that such breach materially increased the risk of loss under the policy as a matter of law. Starting with the text of the PSE, the PSE contains two components relevant here: (1) a requirement that the property feature "operational" smoke detectors and (2) a requirement that those smoke detectors be located in the property's "units and common areas." As neither term is defined in the policy, their definition turns on common usage and "the reasonable expectations of the average insured upon reading the policy" ( Matter of Mostow v State Farm Ins. Cos. , 88 NY2d 321, 326-327 [1996]). Common usage indicates that an operational smoke detector is "ready for or in condition to undertake a destined function" (Merriam-Webster.com Dictionary, operational [https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/operational]), namely, detecting smoke and alerting nearby occupants to its presence ( see Binh Nguyen v Prime Residential Bronx R & R V LLC ,

leads.caseName: Portage Township of St. Joseph County, Indiana v. City of South Bend
leads.text:
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 1 of 8 

Pursuant to Ind. Appellate Rule 65(E), the trial court and parties shall not take any 
action in reliance upon this Opinion until it is certified. 

IN THE 
Court of Appeals of Indiana 

Portage Township of St. Joseph County, Indiana, and 350 
Columbia Street, LLC, 
Appellants-Intervenor Defendants 
v. 
City of South Bend, 
Appellee-Plaintiff 
October 29, 2026 
Court of Appeals Case No. 
26A-PL-711 
Appeal from the Marshall Circuit Court 
The Honorable Janette E. Surrisi, Judge 
Trial Court Cause No. 
50C01-2501-PL-4 

Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 2 of 8 

Opinion by Judge Vaidik 
Judge May concurs. 
Chief Judge Tavitas concurs in result with separate opinion. 
Vaidik, Judge. 
Case Summary 
[1] Indiana law grants units of local government—counties, municipalities, and 
townships—broad eminent-domain power. Indiana Code section 36-7-14-20 
addresses the use of this power in “redevelopment project areas.” Specifically, 
the statute provides that if a unit’s legislative body (e.g., a city council) 
considers it necessary to use eminent domain to acquire real property in a 
redevelopment project area, it must adopt a resolution setting forth that 
determination and directing its attorney to file suit. The issue we must decide in 
this appeal is whether this statute gives a unit’s legislative body exclusive 
authority to exercise the power of eminent domain in a redevelopment project 
area, thereby precluding other unit officials from doing so. We hold that it does. 
Here, the trial court allowed a city to bring an eminent-domain action for 
property in a redevelopment project area without authorization from the city’s 
legislative body, so we reverse. 
Facts and Procedural History 
[2] In October 2024, the City of South Bend, acting at the direction of its mayor, 
filed a Complaint for Condemnation as to real property owned by Argos 316, 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 3 of 8 

LLC. The property is in a redevelopment project area established by the South 
Bend Redevelopment Commission. Portage Township of St. Joseph County 
had previously contracted to buy the property and completed the purchase 
shortly after the City filed its complaint. The Township, along with 350 
Columbia Street, LLC, which held easements on the property, intervened in the 
case and filed objections to the condemnation. As relevant here, Portage 
Township and 350 Columbia Street (“Objectors”) objected under Indiana Code 
section 36-7-14-20(a), which provides: 
If the legislative body of the unit that established the department 
of redevelopment considers it necessary to acquire real property 
in a redevelopment project area by the exercise of the power of 
eminent domain, the legislative body shall adopt a resolution 
setting out its determination to exercise that power and directing 
its attorney to file a petition in the name of the unit on behalf of 
the department of redevelopment, in the circuit or superior court 
of the county in which the property is situated. 
Objectors claimed that the City’s condemnation action is illegal because it was 
not authorized by the South Bend Common Council—the City’s legislative 
body—as contemplated by this statute. After briefing and oral argument, the 
trial court overruled this objection and the others. The court concluded that 
Common Council authorization under Section 36-7-14-20 is just one way, not 
the only way, for the City to use eminent domain to acquire real property in a 
redevelopment project area. 
[3] Objectors now appeal. 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 4 of 8 

Discussion and Decision 
[4] Objectors contend that the trial court erred by overruling their objection under 
Section 36-7-14-20.1 The trial court’s decision turned on the interpretation of 
that statute, which is a pure question of law, so our review is de novo. See 
Anderson v. Gaudin, 42 N.E.3d 82, 85 (Ind. 2015). When a statute is clear and 
unambiguous, no interpretation is necessary; we simply “apply the words and 
phrases in their plain, ordinary, and usual sense.” Id. But when a statute is 
susceptible to more than one interpretation, it is ambiguous and thus open to 
judicial construction. Id. In construing an ambiguous statute, our goal is to 
determine, give effect to, and implement the intent of the Legislature. Id. 
[5] Objectors argue that only the legislative body of a unit of local government can 
exercise the power of eminent domain in a redevelopment project area. They do 
not dispute that units have broad eminent-domain power or that this power can 
generally be exercised by officials other than the unit’s legislative body. See Ind. 
Code § 36-1-4-5(a) (“A unit may acquire by eminent domain or other means, 
and own interests in real and personal property.”). But they assert that Section 
36-7-14-20(a) unambiguously limits the use of eminent domain in the context of 
redevelopment project areas. As noted above, the statute provides that “[i]f the 
legislative body of the unit that established the department of redevelopment 
considers it necessary to acquire real property in a redevelopment project area 

1 Objectors also challenge the overruling of their other objections. Because we reverse based on Section 36-7-
14-20, we need not address those arguments. 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 5 of 8 

by the exercise of the power of eminent domain,” it must adopt a resolution 
setting forth that determination and directing its attorney to file suit. According 
to Objectors, the clear implication of the statute’s language—establishing a 
procedure for a unit’s legislative body to exercise the power of eminent domain 
in a redevelopment project area, but not establishing a procedure for other unit 
officials to exercise that power—is that other officials do not have the power. 
[6] The City also argues that Section 36-7-14-20(a) is unambiguous, but in a much 
different way. The City contends that the statute does nothing to limit who can 
exercise a unit’s power of eminent domain in a redevelopment project area; it 
simply establishes the procedure to be employed “if” it is the unit’s legislative 
body that wants to exercise that power. According to the City, because the 
statute doesn’t expressly state that only a unit’s legislative body can exercise the 
power of eminent domain in a redevelopment project area, or that other unit 
officials cannot exercise such power, the statute has no impact on the broad 
eminent-domain powers of other officials under Indiana Code section 36-1-4-
5(a). In sum, the City maintains that Section 36-7-14-20(a) is merely a 
procedural statute applicable to a unit’s legislative body, not a substantive 
statute establishing who does or does not have the power of eminent domain in 
a redevelopment project area. 
[7] When the statute is read in isolation, both interpretations are reasonable. 
Therefore, the statute is ambiguous, and we must look beyond its plain text to 
discern its meaning. See Anderson, 42 N.E.3d at 85. Having done so, we 
conclude that Objectors offer the correct interpretation. 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 6 of 8 

[8] Section 36-7-14-20 is part of Indiana Code chapter 36-7-14, which establishes a 
comprehensive scheme for units of local government (except townships) to (1) 
create redevelopment project areas and (2) acquire real property in such areas. 
A unit may establish a department of redevelopment, to be controlled by a 
redevelopment commission. I.C. § 36-7-14-3. In turn, a redevelopment 
commission can establish a redevelopment project area for an “area needing 
redevelopment” (with the approval of the unit’s plan commission and legislative 
body). I.C. §§ 36-7-14-15, -16, -17. Once a redevelopment commission 
establishes such an area, it must identify the real property that needs to be 
acquired for the redevelopment project and then attempt to negotiate the 
purchase of that property. I.C. § 36-7-14-19; see also I.C. § 36-7-14-19.5. 
[9] Of course, a redevelopment commission won’t always be able to negotiate an 
amicable purchase of property. And that is when eminent domain becomes 
necessary and Section 36-7-14-20 comes into play. The statute sets forth how 
the power of eminent domain can be exercised in a redevelopment project 
area—through a vote of the unit’s legislative body. While other unit officials 
generally have broad eminent-domain power, and Section 36-7-14-20 doesn’t 
expressly bar them from exercising that power in a redevelopment project area, 
the redevelopment statutory scheme as a whole makes clear that the power lies 
with the unit’s legislative body. Since the property at issue here is in a 
redevelopment project area, and the City’s legislative body didn’t authorize the 
condemnation action, the trial court erred by overruling the objection. 
[10] Reversed. 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 7 of 8 

May, J., concurs. 
Tavitas, C.J., concurs in result with separate opinion. 
ATTORNEY FOR APPELLANTS 
James A. Masters 
Nemeth, Feeney, Masters & Campiti, P.C. 
South Bend, Indiana 

ATTORNEYS FOR APPELLEE 
Jenny R. Buchheit 
Andrew J. Miroff 
John D. French 
Abby V. DeMare 
Ice Miller LLP 
Indianapolis, Indiana 

Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-711 | October 29, 2026 Page 8 of 8 

Tavitas, Chief Judge, concurring in result. 
[11] I concur in result. The majority concludes that Indiana Code Section 36-7-14-
20(a) is ambiguous, but it nevertheless concludes that the authority to exercise 
the power of eminent domain in a redevelopment project area lies with the 
unit’s legislative body. 
[12] Neither party argues that the statute is ambiguous. I am, therefore, hesitant to 
conclude that the statute is ambiguous sua sponte. But because the City’s 
legislative body did not authorize the condemnation action, I agree that the trial 
court erred by overruling the objection.

leads.caseName: RJ's International Trading, LLC v. Crown Castle South, LLC
leads.text:
Supreme Court of Florida
 ____________

 No. SC2024-0547
 ____________

 RJ’S INTERNATIONAL TRADING, LLC,
 Appellant,

 vs.

 CROWN CASTLE SOUTH, LLC, et al.,
 Appellee.

 October 29, 2026

GROSSHANS, J.

 Individuals can transfer land or establish legal interests in it

by executing deeds, contracts, and other documents. Often, such

instruments also impose continuing obligations. Not surprisingly,

these obligations are generally enforceable by and against the

original parties as a matter of contract law. But are those same

contractual obligations binding upon subsequent parties who

acquire an interest in the relevant land? The answer depends, in

part, on how closely the obligation is connected to the land itself.

Where a sufficient connection exists and other requirements are
 satisfied, the obligation binds successors by operation of law and is

said to “run with the land”—an ancient term of art.

 In this case, the parties request that we answer a certified

question from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit,

which asks whether a prevailing-party attorney’s fee provision in an

easement agreement runs with the land as a matter of Florida law.

RJ’s Int’l Trading, LLC v. Crown Castle S., LLC, 98 F.4th 1330, 1343

(11th Cir. 2024). 1 Framed differently, is a promise to pay attorney’s

fees an obligation that binds successors to the land? We conclude

that it is not. In so holding, we decline to extend the reasoning of

our recent decision in Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp., 336 So. 3d 207

(Fla. 2022), which addressed a materially different obligation.

 I

 More than three decades ago, Hidden Valley Corporation

bought two neighboring properties in Miami. Hidden Valley leased

one of them to BellSouth Mobility, later giving BellSouth (and its

successors) permission to use for telecommunication purposes a

portion of the adjacent property (which Hidden Valley retained). In

 1. We have jurisdiction. See art. V, § 3(b)(6), Fla. Const.

 -2-
 the easement agreement creating this nonpossessory interest, there

is a section entitled “Remedies for Breach,” which includes an

attorney’s fee provision. It states:

 In the event that it is necessary for either party hereto to
 file suit in order to enforce the terms hereof, then the
 prevailing party in such suit shall be entitled to receive
 reasonable attorney’s fees and court costs in addition to
 any other award that the court might make, from the
 non-prevailing party.

 Following creation of the easement, multiple transfers of both

properties occurred. At the time of the lawsuit in this case, RJ’s

International Trading, LLC (RJI) owned one of the properties subject

to the easement. Crown Castle South, LLC subleased the

neighboring property from BellSouth and had the right to use a

portion of RJI’s property by virtue of the easement.

 Conflict arose in 2020 when Crown Castle excavated portions

of RJI’s land beyond the easement and installed fiber optic cables

underground. Based on the unauthorized excavation and

installation, RJI sued Crown Castle in federal court. RJI asserted

five claims, alleging trespass and breach of the easement agreement

as two of the theories of liability.

 -3-
  The district court granted partial summary judgment for RJI,

finding Crown Castle liable on the trespass and breach-of-easement

claims. In doing so, the court ruled that a valid and enforceable

easement existed. It further ruled that Crown Castle’s excavation

and installation activities exceeded the easement’s boundaries and

constituted a trespass. The court made no determination as to

damages.

 Ultimately, following a six-day trial, the jury awarded RJI $1

for Crown Castle’s breach of the easement agreement and $40,000

for its trespass. 2 The district court entered a final judgment (later

amended), which reflected the jury’s assigned damages for the

breach-of-easement and trespass claims. 3 Crown Castle did not

seek appellate review.

 After entry of the updated judgment, RJI asked the district

court for an award of attorney’s fees based on the prevailing-party

provision in the easement agreement. Relying on property-law

 2. The jury declined to award any punitive damages.

 3. The jury awarded RJI a small amount of damages for its
last remaining claim, but RJI dismissed that claim prior to entry of
the final judgment.

 -4-
 principles, RJI reasoned that the fee provision was a “real covenant”

that bound not only the original contracting parties (Hidden Valley

and BellSouth) but also those who succeeded them in interest

(including RJI and Crown Castle). Recognizing what Florida law

requires in this regard, RJI contended that the provision ran with

the land.

 Crown Castle opposed RJI’s motion for fees, arguing that the

fee provision was too attenuated from the land to “touch and

concern” it—one of the requirements for a provision to run with the

land. Instead, according to Crown Castle, the fee provision was

merely a personal covenant that bound only the original parties to

the easement agreement: Hidden Valley and BellSouth.

 Siding with Crown Castle, the court denied RJI’s motion for

attorney’s fees. It ruled that the promise to pay attorney’s fees did

not touch and concern land and, thus, did not run with the land.

In reaching this conclusion, the court noted out-of-state cases,

found support in Caulk v. Orange County, 661 So. 2d 932 (Fla. 5th

DCA 1995), and distinguished our decision in Hayslip.

 RJI appealed. The Eleventh Circuit first considered and

rejected RJI’s argument that it was a “part[y] hereto” as that term is

 -5-
 used in the easement agreement. RJ’s Int’l Trading, 98 F.4th at

1339. That interpretive issue is not before us.

 Having resolved this issue against RJI, the court next assessed

whether the prevailing-party fee provision could be enforced as a

covenant running with the land. Id. at 1339-43. It discussed

Florida law on this topic, including Caulk and Hayslip. In Caulk,

the Fifth District Court of Appeal held that the reservation of

eminent-domain proceeds did not run with the land. 661 So. 2d at

934. Hayslip, on the other hand, involved an arbitration provision,

which we found to touch and concern the land. 336 So. 3d at 210.

In the Eleventh Circuit’s view, Hayslip appeared to come closer to

answering the question in this case. RJ’s Int’l Trading, 98 F.4th at

1342. Yet, due to factual distinctions, the court was reluctant to

treat Hayslip as controlling. Id. at 1341-42.

 Based on this uncertainty and other considerations, the

Eleventh Circuit certified the following question to us: “Under

Florida law, when an easement agreement contains a prevailing-

party attorney’s fee provision, is the fee provision a real covenant

such that it runs with the land?” Id. at 1343. We accepted review.

 -6-
  II

 A covenant or obligation that “runs with the land” binds

successors who “become liable as promisors upon the promise

made by their predecessor” by virtue of their acquiring an interest

in the land. Restatement (First) of Prop. § 530 cmt. a (A.L.I. 1944).

Note that this liability is not based on any promise or covenant that

the successor to the land personally made. Id.; see also Huck v.

Kenmare Commons Homes Ass’n, 382 So. 3d 759, 766 (Fla. 1st DCA

2023). Invoking this doctrine, RJI maintains that the attorney’s fee

provision here runs with the land and is binding on Crown Castle

as a matter of Florida law, even though Crown Castle did not

personally promise to pay RJI’s attorney’s fees. Based on our

assessment of the law, we disagree.

 For a covenant to run with the land, three requirements must

be satisfied. First, the original contracting parties must intend for

successors in interest to be bound by the covenant. Hayslip, 336

So. 3d at 209. Second, successors in interest must have notice of

the covenant. Id. And third, the covenant must touch and concern

the land. Id. Our focus is on the final requirement, which is

dispositive in answering the certified question.

 -7-
  A

 Many jurists trace the touch and concern requirement back to

a 1583 English decision, known as Spencer’s Case, 5 Co. Rep. 16a,

77 Eng. Rep. 72 (Q.B. 1583). 4 In that decision, which arose in the

landlord-tenant context, an English court distinguished between

covenants that touched and concerned the land and those that were

merely collateral to it. Spencer’s Case, 5 Co. Rep. at 16b, 77 Eng.

Rep. at 74. The former could be enforceable against an assignee;

the latter could not. To illustrate the distinction, the court

identified several collateral covenants that would not bind an

assignee including: (1) a lessee’s promise to build a house for the

lessor on land that was not the subject of the lease and (2) a

lessee’s promise to pay “any collateral sum” to the lessor. Id.

 Two centuries later, that same English court explained that to

touch and concern 5 the land, the covenant must “directly affect[]

the nature, quality, or value of the thing demised, [or] the mode of

 4. E.g., A. Dan Tarlock, Touch and Concern Is Dead, Long Live
the Doctrine, 77 Neb. L. Rev. 804, 814 (1998); Gallagher v. Bell, 516
A.2d 1028, 1032 (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 1986).

 5. Since its earliest references, courts have used “touch or
concern” and “touch and concern” interchangeably.

 -8-
 occupying it.” Mayor of Congleton v. Pattison, 10 East, 130, 136,

103 Eng. Rep. 725, 727 (K.B. 1808).

 In America, states accepted this common law concept as a

limitation on the enforceability of covenants by or against

successors. See Regency Homes Ass’n v. Egermayer, 498 N.W.2d

783, 789-91 (Neb. 1993) (canvassing cases on this concept from a

multitude of jurisdictions); Flying Diamond Oil Corp. v. Newton

Sheep Co., 776 P.2d 618, 623 (Utah 1989) (noting effect of the touch

and concern requirement). As for Florida, the first reported

decision applying this requirement appears to be Dunn v. Barton, 16

Fla. 765 (1878). There, while not using the specific phrase “touch

and concern,” we found that a restrictive covenant ran with the

land because it affected “the mode of enjoyment of the premises.”

Id. at 771.

 Since then, Florida courts have considered whether certain

covenants or obligations meet the touch and concern requirement.

Caulk, 661 So. 2d at 933 (reservation of right to proceeds from an

eminent-domain proceeding); Maule Indus., Inc. v. Sheffield Steel

Prods., Inc., 105 So. 2d 798, 799 (Fla. 3d DCA 1958) (covenant

requiring maintenance of railroad facilities); Hagan v. Sabal Palms,

 -9-
 Inc., 186 So. 2d 302, 304 (Fla. 2d DCA 1966) (covenant restricting

what buildings could be constructed); Huck, 382 So. 3d at 766

(prohibition on street parking); Keyes Co. v. Frazier, 213 So. 2d 276,

277 (Fla. 3d DCA 1968) (promise to pay real estate commission);

Winn-Dixie Stores, Inc. v. Dolgencorp, Inc., 964 So. 2d 261, 262 (Fla.

4th DCA 2007) (restricting commercial use of certain property).

 In some cases, courts spoke in terms of the obligation

enhancing the value of the land. E.g., Maule Indus., 105 So. 2d at

801. But in those same cases and others, courts focused on

whether the covenant affected the use, occupation, or enjoyment of

the land. Dunn, 16 Fla. at 771; Maule Indus., 105 So. 2d at 801;

Winn-Dixie Stores, 964 So. 2d at 265; Huck, 382 So. 3d at 765. We

think that this latter formulation is doctrinally sound and

consistent with the concept’s history. Accordingly, when deciding if

the touch and concern requirement is met, courts should consider

whether the obligation is sufficiently connected to how the land is

used, occupied, or enjoyed.

 B

 Florida courts have not previously considered the particular

obligation at issue here. That being said, we believe that Caulk—a

 - 10 -
 case we cited with approval in Hayslip—provides helpful insight.

The covenant at issue in Caulk reserved to the original grantor

proceeds from any eminent-domain pro

leads.text:
[J-39-2026]
 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA
 MIDDLE DISTRICT

TODD, C.J., DONOHUE, DOUGHERTY, WECHT, MUNDY, BROBSON, McCAFFERY, JJ.

 GARY WHITTINGTON AND DONNA : No. 47 MAP 2025
 WHITTINGTON, :
 : Appeal from the Order of the
 Appellants : Superior Court at No. 1734 MDA
 : 2022 dated February 19, 2025
 : Affirming the Judgment of the
 v. : Franklin County Court of Common
 : Pleas, Civil Division, at No. 2017-
 : 02792 dated January 31, 2023
 JOE DANIELS, :
 : ARGUED: May 19, 2026
 Appellee :

 OPINION

 JUSTICE MUNDY DECIDED: October 29, 2026
 Appellants Gary and Donna Whittington (collectively the Whittingtons) filed an

 action against their contractor in magisterial district court before a magisterial district

 judge (collectively MDJ or MDJ court) for the return of a deposit paid for the construction

 of a house that was never built. In an issue of first impression, we consider what impact

 the filing of a complaint in MDJ court (MDJ complaint) has on the tolling of the statute of

 limitations. After consideration of the Judicial Code and the Pennsylvania Rules of Civil

 Procedure Governing Actions and Proceedings Before Magisterial District Judges (MDJ

 Rules), we conclude that the filing of an MDJ complaint tolls the statute of limitations for

 any cause of action based on the factual averments in that complaint. The holding of the

 Superior Court is therefore reversed.
  Because this case originated with the filing of an MDJ complaint that was

subsequently appealed to the court of common pleas, we begin with a brief review of that

process. Civil matters in our MDJ courts are governed by the MDJ Rules. Pursuant to

these rules, an “‘action’ means a civil action brought before a magisterial district judge”

and includes any action within the MDJ’s jurisdiction, except an action by a landlord

against a tenant for the recovery of the possession of real property (MDJ action).

Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 301(a), (b). An MDJ action is commenced by the filing of an MDJ

complaint and the commencement of an action by summons is not permitted.

Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 303, Note. The form and contents of an MDJ complaint are also

detailed in the MDJ rules. An MDJ complaint shall be in writing on a form prescribed by

the State Court Administrator, Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 304(A), and shall set forth:

 (1) The names and addresses of the parties.

 (2) The amount claimed.

 (3) A brief and concise statement of the facts upon which the claim is based
 including:

 a. The date, time and place of the occurrence and a brief description
 of the damages sustained when the claim alleges tortious
 conduct; or

 b. The date of the transaction and a brief description of the subject
 matter when the claim is contractual;

 c. the date and description of the occurrence when the claim is for
 a civil fine or penalty and the citation to the statute authorizing the
 claim.

 (4) Such other information as shall be required on the complaint form.
Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 304(B).

 When the MDJ court holds a hearing on an MDJ complaint “[j]udgment shall be

given at the conclusion of the hearing or within five (5) days thereafter and shall be

 [J-39-2026] - 2
 entered on the complaint form.” Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 322. If the judgment is for money

damages, an aggrieved party may appeal by filing a notice of appeal with the prothonotary

of the court of common pleas within thirty days after entry of the judgment.

Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 1002(A). After the filing of a notice of appeal, a complaint must be

filed in the court of common pleas (common pleas court complaint):

 A. If the appellant was the claimant in the action before the magisterial
 district judge, he shall file a complaint within twenty (20) days after filing
 his notice of appeal.

 B. If the appellant was the defendant in the action before the magisterial
 district judge, he shall file with his notice of appeal a praecipe requesting
 the prothonotary to enter a rule as of course upon the appellee to file a
 complaint within twenty (20) days after service of the rule or suffer entry
 of a judgment of non pros.

 C. When judgments have been rendered on complaints of both the appellant
 and the appellee and the appellant appeals from the judgment on his
 complaint or on both complaints, the appellee may assert his claim in the
 court of common pleas by pleading it as a counterclaim if it can properly
 be so pleaded in that court. If the appellant appeals only from the
 judgment of his complaint, the appellee may appeal from the judgment
 on his complaint at any time within thirty (30) days after the date on which
 the appellant served a copy of his notice of appeal upon the appellee.
Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 1004. On appeal, the proceedings shall be conducted de novo and be

subject to the Rules of Civil Procedure that would be applicable if the action was originally

commenced in the court of common pleas. Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 1007(A). Additionally,

except in very limited circumstances as provided by the MDJ rules, “the action upon

appeal may not be limited with respect to amount in controversy, joinder of causes of

action or parties, counterclaims, added or changed averments or otherwise because of

the particulars of the action before the magisterial district judge.” Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J.

1007(B).

 In this case, the Whittingtons contracted with Appellee Joe Daniels (Daniels) for

the construction of a new home in Franklin County, Pennsylvania on April 29, 2015. As

 [J-39-2026] - 3
 part of the contract, the Whittingtons paid Daniels a ten-thousand-dollar deposit. On or

about October 5, 2015, however, the Whittingtons gave Daniels written notice cancelling

the contract. Upon cancellation, the Whittingtons initially believed Daniels would return

their ten-thousand-dollar deposit but became aware Daniels intended to retain the deposit

after a phone call between the parties later in October. As a result of Daniels’ retention

of the deposit, on April 10, 2017, the Whittingtons filed an MDJ complaint. That complaint

read, in full, “[Daniels] failed to return our deposit of [$]10,000 for upgrades on a house

which he never built upon our termination of the contract.” MDJ Complaint, 4/10/17. On

June 27, 2017, after a hearing, the MDJ entered judgment in the Whittingtons’ favor for

ten thousand dollars plus costs. Daniels filed a timely Notice of Appeal of the MDJ

judgment in the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas on July 13, 2017. The Notice

of Appeal included the required praecipe to the prothonotary to enter a rule upon

Appellants to file a common pleas court complaint within twenty days. Notice of Appeal,

7/13/17. The prothonotary entered a rule that informed the Whittingtons that if they did

not file a common pleas court complaint within this timeframe, a “judgment of non pros

may be entered against” them. Id. (capitalization removed).

 The Whittingtons did not file a common pleas court complaint within the twenty-

day time period, nor did Daniels file a motion for entry of a judgment of non pros. Instead,

the case remained dormant until July 1, 2020, when the common pleas court entered a

Notice of Intent to Terminate Case and Remove it From the Civil Docket (Notice of Intent

to Terminate), notifying the parties that, unless they filed a written objection to termination

or a statement of intent to proceed, the court would issue an order terminating the case

and directing the prothonotary to mark the case as terminated from the docket. Notice of

Intent to Terminate, 7/1/20. In response, the Whittingtons filed a Statement of Intent to

Proceed and a common pleas court complaint on July 10, 2020. In their common pleas

 [J-39-2026] - 4
 court complaint, the Whittingtons raised four counts, including a claim for

misappropriation/conversion, in which they asserted that Daniels, by retaining their ten-

thousand-dollar deposit, converted funds rightfully belonging to Appellants without their

consent. See Common Pleas Court Complaint, 7/10/20, ¶¶ 37-46. Daniels filed an

Answer with New Matter and Counterclaims (Answer), asserting, inter alia, that the

Whittingtons’ claims were barred by the statute of limitations because they did not file

their common pleas court complaint until July 9, 2020. Answer, 8/21/20, ¶ 47.

 After discovery and pre-trial motions, the case proceeded to a jury trial. The jury

returned a verdict in the Whittingtons’ favor on their conversion claim and in Daniels’ favor

on all other counts. The jury additionally found that the date of accrual of the Whittingtons’

conversion cause of action was October 15, 2015. Based on that finding, Daniels moved

for a directed verdict. Relying on the jury’s determination of the date of the accrual and

the fact that the Whittingtons did not file their common pleas court complaint until July 10,

2020, the trial court determined that the Whittingtons failed to file their complaint within

the two-year statute of limitations period for a conversion action and granted Daniels’

request, entering judgment in his favor. After their motion for reconsideration was denied,

the Whittingtons timely appealed.

 Before the Superior Court the Whittingtons challenged, inter alia, 1 the trial court’s

entry of a directed verdict based on the statute of limitations. In a published opinion, a

unanimous Superior Court panel affirmed. See Whittington v. Daniels, 332 A.3d 102 (Pa.

Super. 2025). The Whittingtons maintained that their action was timely because they filed

their MDJ complaint within the applicable statute of limitations and that Daniels failed to

1 The Whittingtons also raised two other issues related to the trial court’s denial of their

motion for a directed verdict and the issuance of jury instructions as to the statute of
limitations. The Superior Court affirmed the trial court’s decision on those issues, and
they are not currently before the Court.

 [J-39-2026] - 5
 perfect his appeal of the MDJ judgment with the court of common pleas. Daniels

countered that filing an MDJ complaint is not the equivalent of filing a writ of summons or

a common pleas court complaint and therefore does not toll the statute of limitations.

 The court recognized that the question of whether the filing of an MDJ complaint

tolls the statute of limitations was a matter of first impression. Id. at 109. Rejecting

Daniels’ restrictive position, the court determined that holding that the filing of an MDJ

complaint does not toll the statute of limitations at all would be at odds with its prior

jurisprudence concerning the effects of filing MDJ actions. Id. at 110. In this vein, the

court discussed its prior holding in A.C. Elfman & Sons, Inc. v. Clime, 513 A.2d 488 (Pa.

Super. 1986), where it opined “where the doctrine of res judicata is otherwise applicable,

its invocation will not be precluded or impaired because the prior judgment was entered

in an [MDJ] action.” Id. (quoting Elfman, 513 A.2d at 490); see also id. (citing Durand v.

JR Beard, LLC, 2023 WL 6366708 (Pa. Super. filed Sept. 29, 2023) (unpublished

memorandum) (holding that where neither party appealed an MDJ judgment res judicata

barred a subsequent civil complaint arising from the same set of facts). According to the

panel, based on these cases, it would be inconsistent to hold that MDJ actions “have a

preclusive effect on future litigation but that they have no effect on the statute of

limitations.” Id. The court, however, also rejected the Whittingtons’ maximalist argument

that filing an MDJ complaint indefinitely tolls the statute of limitations. Rather, the panel

concluded that the filing of an MDJ complaint “tolls the statute of limitations during the

pendency of that case. However, if a defendant perfects an appeal and properly serves

the plaintiff with a praecipe to file a complaint, the statute of limitations begins to run again

at the expiration of the twenty-day period in which the plaintiff is require

NOTICE: All slip opinions and orders are subject to formal 
revision and are superseded by the advance sheets and bound 
volumes of the Official Reports. If you find a typographical 
error or other formal error, please notify the Reporter of 
Decisions, Supreme Judicial Court, John Adams Courthouse, 1 
Pemberton Square, Suite 2500, Boston, MA, 02108-1750; (617) 557-
1030; SJCReporter@sjc.state.ma.us 

SJC-13964 

ROBERT GAMBEE vs. WELLS FARGO BANK, N.A., & another.1 

October 29, 2026. 

Supreme Judicial Court, Superintendence of inferior courts. 

The petitioner, Robert Gambee, appeals from a judgment of 
the county court denying his petition for relief under G. L. 
c. 211, § 3. We affirm. 
This matter arises from the foreclosure of Gambee's 
Nantucket residence in 2010. Beginning in 2013, Gambee 
commenced the first of five separate lawsuits challenging the 
foreclosure. Each one has been unsuccessful. Among these was a 
2016 action in the Land Court. Seven years after that matter 
was dismissed, Gambee filed a motion for relief from judgment 
pursuant to Mass. R. Civ. P. 60 (b) (6), 365 Mass. 828 (1974). 
In support of the motion, Gambee asserted that he had since 
obtained proof that the foreclosure had been conducted by a bank 
that never received any ownership interest in the home, an 
allegation that he characterized as newly discovered evidence. 
He further argued that this evidence established that one or 
both of the defendants in that matter (who are the respondents 
in the present action) had engaged in fraud. A judge in the 
Land Court denied the motion as untimely, observing that Gambee 
was seeking relief based on information he claimed to have 
obtained six years prior to filing the motion. On March 13, 
2025, Gambee filed a complaint in the Superior Court based upon 
the same factual assertions that had served as the basis for the 
aforementioned motion. The Superior Court dismissed the 
complaint under the doctrine of res judicata. The court also 

1 HSBC BANK USA, N.A., as trustee for MLMI 2006-AF2. 
2 

granted the defendants' request for entry of an order 
prohibiting Gambee from filing any additional complaints in the 
Superior Court without authorization from the regional 
administrative justice. Gambee subsequently filed a motion 
requesting leave to file a motion to vacate the Superior Court 
judgment, citing rule 60 (b) (6). That motion was denied. On 
May 19, 2026, Gambee filed the instant petition seeking relief 
from the aforementioned Superior Court orders. A single justice 
of this court denied the petition without a hearing, and this 
appeal followed. 
Gambee has submitted a memorandum and appendix pursuant to 
S.J.C. Rule 2:21, as amended, 434 Mass. 1301 (2001), which 
requires a petitioner seeking relief from an interlocutory 
ruling of the trial court to "set forth the reasons why review 
of the trial court decision cannot adequately be obtained on 
appeal from any final adverse judgment in the trial court or by 
other available means." Because Gambee principally contests the 
dismissal of his civil action by the Superior Court, rule 2:21 
does not technically apply. See Spencer v. Beacon Hill Hotel, 
448 Mass. 1017, 1017 (2007); Gianopoulos v. Clerk-Magistrate of 
the Attleboro Div. of the Dist. Court Dep't, 446 Mass. 1002, 
1003 (2006). Regardless of the applicability of the rule, 
however, Gambee is not entitled to relief under G. L. c. 211, 
§ 3, unless he can establish the absence of an adequate 
alternative remedy. See Darby v. Commonwealth, 494 Mass. 1023, 
1023 (2024). Gambee cannot do so here. 
In his memorandum, Gambee argues that a direct appeal from 
the dismissal of his complaint does not provide an adequate 
alternative remedy because the "correct vehicle" for 
adjudicating his claim is a motion for relief from judgment 
under rule 60 (b) (6). As indicated, he filed one such motion 
in the Land Court and sought leave to do the same in the 
Superior Court, based on his assertions about fraud and newly 
discovered evidence. Both motions were denied, and Gambee did 
not appeal. " The fact that the petitioner failed to pursue [an] 
alternative route or pursued it unsuccessfully does not create a 
right to relief under G. L. c. 211, § 3" (quotation and citation 
omitted). Tavares v. Commonwealth, 481 Mass. 1044, 1045 (2019). 
Because Gambee could have sought appellate relief in the 
ordinary course, the single justice did not commit an error of 
law or abuse his discretion by denying extraordinary relief 
under G. L. c. 211, § 3. See Matter of an Impounded Case (No. 
4), 497 Mass. 1036, 1038 (2026) (affirming denial of petition 
under G. L. c. 211, § 3, where petitioner could have appealed 
judgment in ordinary course, as well as denial of rule 60 
3 

motion). See also Cooper v. CVS Pharmacy, 450 Mass. 1024, 1025 
(2008) (petitioner seeking relief from Superior Court order 
prohibiting him from filing claims without approval of regional 
administrative justice failed to demonstrate absence of adequate 
alternative remedies). 
 Judgment affirmed. 

 The case was submitted on the papers filed, accompanied by 
a memorandum of law. 
 Robert Gambee, pro se.

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF TENNESSEE
AT JACKSON
October 2, 2025 Session
COMMERCIAL PAINTING COMPANY INC. v. THE WEITZ COMPANY 
LLC ET AL.
Appeal from the Chancery Court for Shelby County
No. CH-06-1573 JoeDae L. Jenkins, Chancellor
___________________________________
No. W2019-02089-COA-R3-CV
___________________________________
The Tennessee Supreme Court remanded this case, directing this court to determine 
whether the parties’ contractual waiver applied to punitive damages that were awarded in 
connection with a tort claim for intentional misrepresentation. W e conclude that the 
contractual waiver in this case is not a bar to the punitive damages awarded for intentional 
misrepresentation. The trial court’s judgment on this matter is affirmed. 
Tenn. R. App. P. 3 Appeal as of Right; Judgment of the Chancery Court Affirmed
JEFFREY USMAN, J., delivered the opinion of the court, in which J. STEVEN STAFFORD, P.J.,
W.S., and CARMA DENNIS MCGEE, J., joined.
Philip E. Beck, Atlanta, Georgia; Jeffrey C. Smith, Memphis, Tennessee; and John A. 
Templer, Jr., Des Moines, Iowa, for the appellants, The Weitz Company, LLC, Federal 
Insurance Company (NJ), and St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company.
Scott A. Frick, Memphis, Tennessee, for the appellees, Commercial Painting Company, 
Inc., and Liberty Mutual Insurance Company (MA).
OPINION
I.
Like a relentless vine growing over the course of more than two decades of 
litigation, this case has become ever more tangled — the present appeal being the fifth 
iteration of this case before the Tennessee Court of Appeals. The Tennessee Supreme 
Court sketched out a significant portion of the tortuous journey in the following manner:
10/28/2026

- 2 -
This case stems from a contract dispute between a general contractor, 
The Weitz Company, LLC, and its drywall subcontractor, Commercial 
Painting Company, Inc. Weitz was the general contractor on a multi-building 
retirement community in Shelby County. In December 2004, the parties 
entered into a contract for Commercial Painting to perform drywall work on 
the project.1 The contract included a schedule detailing the phases and timing 
of construction. Weitz agreed to pay Commercial Painting $3,222,400 for 
its work. Change orders later increased the amount to $3,315,189. The 
parties had various disputes as the project progressed.
By the end of the contract, Weitz had paid Commercial Painting 
twelve of its seventeen pay applications. Weitz refused to pay the remaining 
five applications, claiming they were submitted untimely and contained 
improper change order requests.
In August 2006, Commercial Painting sued Weitz2 and its sureties, 
Federal Insurance Company and St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company, 
and The Village at Germantown in the Shelby County Chancery Court 
seeking $1,929,428.74 in damages for breach of contract, including 
attorney’s fees.3 Commercial Painting alleged that Weitz failed to properly 
sequence, coordinate, monitor, and inspect the work of the various 
subcontractors on the project, which caused Commercial Painting extra work 
and forced it to work in a more inefficient and costly manner. The complaint 
also included claims for payment under the performance bond issued by 
Weitz’s sureties, interest on retainage under section 66-11-144 of the 

1 The work included installation of exterior ceiling insulation; exterior wall metal framing; exterior 
wall insulation; light gauge metal partitions; gypsum board walls, ceilings, and soffits; and suspended 
ceilings. T he contract, with an effective date of September 28, 2004, was signed by the president of 
Commercial Painting on November 1, 2004, and by Weitz’s representative on December 7, 2004.
2 The defendant named in the complaint’s caption was The Weitz Company, Inc., but the first 
paragraph of the complaint referenced the defendant as The Weitz Company-National. These entities are 
referred to herein collectively as “Weitz.”
3 Section 12.1 of the contract provides:
In the event it shall become necessary for either party to institute legal proceedings against 
the other party for recovery of any amounts due and owing under the Agreement, it is 
expressly agreed that the prevailing party in any such action shall be entitled to recover 
from the non-prevailing party all costs, including reasonable attorney’s fees, of pre-suit 
collection attempts, suit, and post judgment or settlement collection including those 
incurred on appeal.
- 3 -
Tennessee Code,4 unjust enrichment, enforcement of Commercial Painting’s 
mechanic’s and materialman’s lien, and interest and attorney’s fees under the 
Prompt Pay Act of 1991.5
Weitz answered and counterclaimed against Commercial Painting and 
its surety for “no event less than” $500,000 in damages for costs allegedly 
incurred on the project due to Commercial Painting’s delay and defective 
workmanship.
In a later amendment to its complaint, Commercial Painting asserted 
additional claims for fraud, intentional and negligent misrepresentation, 
rescission/reformation of the contract, and $10,000,000 in punitive damages. 
Commercial Painting alleged Weitz negotiated a six-month extension with 
the project owner before executing the contract with Commercial Painting, 
but the construction schedule attached to the contract did not reflect the 
extension. Commercial Painting also claimed Weitz signed the contract 
knowing the schedule was outdated by about eightmonths and that the actual 
length of the delay was eight to twelve months. Commercial Painting alleged 
that Weitz knew when it executed the contract that to make up for the delay, 
it would have to compress the construction schedule and hire extra workers
to supplement the work of various subcontractors, including Commercial 
Painting’s drywall work. Commercial Painting also asserted that after 
negotiating the six-month extension with the project owner, Weitz issued an 
amended construction schedule that was “fraudulent and unrealistic” in order 
to earn an early completion bonus.6 According to Commercial Painting, 
Weitz continued to issue construction schedules that were unrealistic, and 
required the subcontractors to adhere to those schedules, never revealing the 
actual length of the extension until near the end of the project when it became 
clear that Weitz could not complete construction in time to earn the early 
completion bonus. Commercial Painting contended that Weitz improperly 
supplemented Commercial Painting’s work by falsely claiming Commercial 
Painting was not completing its work according to a schedule that Weitz 
knew contained false information about the project completion date and that 
Weitz fraudulently charged Commercial Painting for the cost of the 
supplemental drywall work. Weitz generally denied the allegations in the 
amended complaint and reiterated the allegations in its counterclaim that 

4 Transferred to section 66-34-104 of the Tennessee Code by 2008 Public Acts, chapter 804, section 
2, effective July 1, 2008.
5 Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 66-34-101 to -704.
6 The extension agreement negotiated by Weitz and the project owner included a bonus to Weitz of 
$8,597 for each day, up to forty-five days, that the project was completed early.
- 4 -
Commercial Painting was in breach of the subcontract and did not perform 
its contractual duties in a timely and workmanlike manner.
The trial court granted partial summary judgment in favor of Weitz on 
Commercial Painting’s claims for intentional/negligent misrepresentation 
and fraud, rescission/reformation of the contract, and punitive damages. 
After a bench trial, the trial court awarded Commercial Painting $450,464.26 
for breach of contract, finding that Commercial Painting was entitled to 
$600,464.26 less a $150,000 offset to Weitz for having to supplement 
Commercial Painting’s work.
The Court of Appeals vacated the trial court’s award of partial 
summary judgment to Weitz, concluding that Commercial Painting 
established a genuine issue of material fact regarding the intentional and 
negligent misrepresentation claims. Com. Painting Co. v. Weitz Co., LLC
[(“Com. Painting I”)], No. W2013-01989-COA-R3-CV, 2016 WL 3519015, 
at *2 (Tenn. Ct. App. June 20, 2016).
Com. Painting Co. Inc. v. Weitz Co.(“Com. Painting B”),7 676 S.W.3d 527, 529-31 (Tenn. 
2023).
The case was appealed, and the Tennessee Supreme Court remanded to this Court 
for reconsideration in light of the changes to the summary judgment standard set forth in
Rye v. Women’s Care Ctr. of Memphis, MPLLC, 477 S.W.3d 235 (Tenn. 2015). Com.
Painting Co., Inc. v. Weitz Co. (“Com. Painting A”), No. W2013-01989-SC-R11-CV 
(Tenn. Nov. 25, 2015) (Order). On remand, this Court concluded that, applying the new 
summary judgment standard, the trial court had erred in granting summary judgment on 
the claims for intentional or negligent misrepresentation; accordingly, this court reversed 
the grant of summary judgment, vacated the judgment and damages from the bench trial, 
and remanded for further proceedings. Com. Painting Co., Inc. v. The Weitz Co. (“Com. 
Painting II”), No. W2013-01989-COA-R3-CV, 2016 WL 3519015, at *1 (Tenn. Ct. App. 
June 20, 2016). In doing so, this court held, “Commercial Painting is entitled to just one 
recovery to the extent damages from more than one cause of action overlap, but it should 
not be precluded from proceeding on multiple theories of liability if it is able to make out 
a prima facie case under more than one cause of action.” Id. at *12. This court noted that 
Commercial Painting was “not required to choose between various causes of action” and 
that it may be entitled to recover punitive damages. Id.
After the remand, Commercial Painting amended its complaint; it sought a jury trial 

7 In order to distinguish the various appellate opinions generated by this litigation, and to maintain 
consistency with the naming used by prior opinions in this case, we designate this court’s four prior opinions 
with Roman numerals, and we designate the Supreme Court’s prior opinions and orders with capital letters.
- 5 -
on claims for negligent and intentional misrepresentation, breach of contract, unjust 
enrichment, and damages pursuant to a payment bond. Com. Painting Co. Inc. v. Weitz 
Co. (“Com. Painting III”), No. W2019-02089-COA-R3-CV, 2022 WL 737468, at *4 
(Tenn. Ct. App. Mar. 11, 2022), rev’d and remanded, 676 S.W.3d 527 (Tenn. 2023). At 
the 2018 jury trial, Commercial Painting presented proof that it was misled by Weitz 
regarding the bids from other subcontractors, the delays in the project, and the extension 
for completion. Id.
In October 2018, the jury returned a verdict for Commercial Painting under four 
theories: breach of contract, unjust enrichment/quantum meruit, intentional 
misrepresentation, and under the payment bond. Com. Painting III, 2022 WL 737468, at 
*5. It awarded $8,359,863.83, which included $1,272,952.46 in compensatory damages, 8
$2,083,362.16 in pre-judgment interest, $1,103,549.00 in attorney’s fees, and $3,900,000 
in punitive damages, plus post-judgment interest. Id. at *5-6.
In affirming the punitive damages, the trial court noted the jury’s finding that the 
elements of fraud were met, that Weitz acted in bad faith, and that Weitz acted 
intentionally, recklessly, maliciously, or fraudulently such that the conduct was egregious. 
The trial court made findings of fact in support of upholding the jury’s punitive damages 
award. It found that, prior to the execution of the subcontract, Weitz was aware that it was 
behind schedule by eight months. Weitz planned to recover the delay by compressing the 
construction schedule and by supplementing the drywall work which had not yet been 
assigned through a subcontract. Although the subcontract had not been executed, Weitz 
told Commercial Painting that it was “imperative” that Commercial Painting’s payment 
and performance bond be issued. Commercial Painting provided evidence that, once

 Electronically Filed
 Supreme Court

 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF HAWAIʻI

 ---o0o---
________________________________________________________________

 MARCUS L. KAWATACHI, in his official capacity as
 Executive Director of the Hawaiʻi Civil Rights Commission,
 ex relatione, ROBERT A. FAHN and BRENDA A. FAHN,
 Respondent/Plaintiff-Appellant,

 vs.

 THE PARRISH COLLECTION, LLC; THE PARRISH COLLECTION KAUAI;
 JONATHAN D. PARRISH and SIMONE McCAFFREY,
 Petitioners/Defendants-Appellees,

 and

 LINDA EVANS, as Trustee of the LAURA P. EVANS
 REVOCABLE TRUST DATED May 8, 2022,
 Respondent/Defendant-Appellee.
________________________________________________________________

 SCWC-XX-XXXXXXX

 CERTIORARI TO THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS
 (CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX; CASE NO. 5CCV-XX-XXXXXXX)

 OCTOBER 28, 2026

 DEVENS, C.J., McKENNA, EDDINS, AND GINOZA, JJ., AND
 CIRCUIT JUDGE DREWYER, ASSIGNED BY REASON OF VACANCY
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 OPINION OF THE COURT BY McKENNA, J.

 I. Introduction

 During the COVID-19 pandemic, a tenant with a disability

requested that a landlord provide an accommodation waiving a

weekly cleanings provision in a rental agreement. The tenant

explained that, because of his disability, he faced an increased

risk of hospitalization or death if he contracted the virus. He

therefore did not want non-family members entering the property.

The landlord denied the request, saying that the accommodation

was neither reasonable nor necessary.

 The Circuit Court of the Fifth Circuit (“circuit court”)

granted summary judgment in favor of the landlord. The

Intermediate Court of Appeals (“ICA”) vacated this judgment and

ordered a remand. On certiorari, the landlord alleges the ICA

erred.

 The ICA did not err by vacating summary judgment. But in

this opinion, we provide guidance on how disability

accommodation requests are to be evaluated under Hawaiʻi’s fair

housing law. We also address an issue not addressed by the ICA.

Although parties are encouraged to engage in an interactive

process, under current law, there is no standalone liability if

there is a breakdown in engagement.

 2
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 We therefore affirm the ICA’s December 17, 2025, judgment

on appeal and remand the case to the circuit court for further

proceedings consistent with this opinion.

 II. Background

A. Legal Background

 1. Formation of the HCRC

 The Hawaiʻi Civil Rights Commission (“HCRC”) was formed

through Act 219, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi 1988, which was codified

as HRS Chapter 368. 1998 Haw. Sess. Laws Act 219, § 1 at 1-3;

see HRS § 368-1 (2015). HCRC is authorized to provide “a

uniform procedure” for enforcing Hawaiʻi’s anti-discrimination

laws in the areas of employment (HRS Chapter 378), housing (HRS

Chapter 515), and public accommodations (HRS Chapter 489). HRS

§ 368-1 (2015); see HRS § 515-9.

 In enacting Chapter 368, the Hawaiʻi State Legislature (the

“Legislature”) found and declared, among other things, that

discrimination in housing is contrary to public policy. Chapter

368 also vests the HCRC with powers to “receive, investigate,

and conciliate complaints;” “hold hearings and make inquiries;”

“commence civil actions in circuit court to seek appropriate

relief;” “issue the right to sue to a complainant;” “order

appropriate legal and equitable relief or affirmative action;”

and “adopt rules.” HRS § 368-3(1)-(5), (9) (2015).

 3
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 2. Hawaiʻi’s Fair Housing Law

 Hawaiʻi’s fair housing law is codified in the Hawaiʻi

Discrimination in Real Property Transactions Act, Hawaiʻi Revised

Statutes (“HRS”) §§ 515 et seq., and Hawaiʻi Administrative Rules

(“HAR”) §§ 12-46-301 et seq. Hawaiʻi’s fair housing law

protects against discrimination on the basis of race, sex

(including gender identity or expression), sexual orientation,

color, religion, marital status, familial status, ancestry,

disability, age, or human immunodeficiency virus infection

(“HIV”). HRS § 515-3(a) (Supp. 2023). Chapter 515 applies to

sales, leases, rentals, and other housing practices, see HRS §§

515-3(a)(1)-(11) and 515-5 (2018), and provides complainants

with substantive rights as well as potential legal and equitable

remedies. See HRS §§ 515-9 (2018) and 515-13 (2018).

 When Chapter 515 was initially promulgated in 1967, the

Legislature directed that it “shall be construed according to

the fair import of its terms and shall be liberally construed.”

HRS § 515-1 (2018).

 Then, in 1992, the Legislature passed Act 171, Session Laws

of Hawaiʻi 1992. The purpose section of Act 171 stated:

 SECTION 1. The purpose of this Act is to conform the Real
 Estate Transactions Law, which prohibits discrimination in
 matters related to housing and real estate, with the
 federal Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988. The Department
 of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) has published notice
 that Hawaiʻi’s law is no longer substantially equivalent to
 federal law. HUD intends to decertify Hawaiʻi unless these
 amendments are enacted. Certification is necessary in order

 4
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 for Hawaiʻi to receive federal funds for the investigation
 of housing discrimination cases.

1992 Haw. Sess. Laws Act 171 § 1 at 1 (“Act 171”).

 The HCRC administers Hawaiʻi’s fair housing law. To

maintain HCRC’s federal certification, HUD requires that “the

fair housing law that the agency administers provide[] rights,

procedures, remedies, and the availability of judicial review

that are substantially equivalent to those provided in the

federal Fair Housing Act.” 24 C.F.R. § 115.201(a) & (b); see

HRS Chapter 368. Act 171 was passed because Hawaiʻi’s fair

housing law was apparently not as protective as the 1988 federal

Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 (“FHAA”), especially with

respect to disability discrimination.

 3. HCRC’s Enforcement of Hawaiʻi’s Fair Housing Law

 As required by Act 171 of 1992, the HCRC promulgated HAR

§§ 12-46-301 et seq. to implement and conform Hawaiʻi’s fair

housing law to Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as

amended by the FHAA. HAR § 12-46-301; 42 U.S.C. §§ 3601-3619;

1992 Haw. Sess. Laws Act 171, § 1 at 1.

 HAR § 12-46-301 states in relevant part:

 The purpose of this subchapter is to implement laws
 prohibiting discrimination in real property transactions
 toward the goal of eliminating such discrimination and to
 implement changes made by Act 171, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi
 1992, to conform state law to Title VIII of the Civil
 Rights Act of 1968, as amended by the Fair Housing
 Amendments Act of 1988. Chapter 515, HRS, prohibits
 discriminatory practices by an owner, any person engaging
 in a real property or real estate transaction, or a real

 5
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 estate broker or salesperson against another person because
 of a protected basis.

 4. Conformance with Federal Law

 Thus, both Act 171 and HAR § 12-46-301 require this court

to construe our fair housing law in conformance with federal law

for HCRC to remain qualified as a certified agency to receive

federal funds for investigation and enforcement work. Hence,

federal caselaw interpreting the FHAA guides this court’s

interpretation of Hawai‘i’s fair housing law.

B. Factual and Procedural Background

 1. Factual Background

 As the founder of the Parrish Collection Kauai, Jonathan

Parrish (collectively, “Parrish”) oversees the management and

operation of high-end vacation rental properties on Kauaʻi.

 In 2006, Robert A. Fahn (“Robert”) was diagnosed with heart

disease. In August 2020, Robert and Brenda A. Fahn (“Brenda”)

(together, the “Fahns”) moved from Colorado to Kauaʻi with their

family because Kauaʻi had relatively few COVID-19 cases.

 In August 2020, the Fahns and Parrish executed a rental

agreement for a rental property in Koloa. The rental agreement

contained a provision governing weekly cleanings of the

property:

 6
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 4. Cleaning to be scheduled every week and completed by the
 Parrish Collection Housekeeping staff and paid for by the
 tenant. This will be done hourly at $40.00 per hour and the
 number of hours dependent on property condition.

(“Weekly Cleanings Provision”)

 Shortly after moving in, Brenda emailed a Parrish employee

that she did not want housekeeping staff entering the property

based on a negative COVID-19 test result. At the time, while

not expressly requesting an accommodation based on Robert’s

heart disease, Brenda explained that Robert “has a 5-6 [percent]

mortality rate and almost 20 [percent] hospital rate (because of

his age and conditions).” Brenda ended with, “I hope you

understand wanting to delay housekeeping.”

 But on November 16, Parrish informed the Fahns that they

failed to comply with the Weekly Cleanings Provision and that

they “cannot be selective” in granting Parrish access for

repairs but not for cleaning.

 Then, on November 23, the Fahns’ doctor sent Parrish a

letter expressly requesting an accommodation through suspension

of the Weekly Cleanings Provision because of Robert’s heart

disease. On November 24, Robert also sent Parrish a letter

formally requesting a waiver of the Weekly Cleanings Provision

based on his disability.

 On November 25, the Fahns’ mainland attorney emailed

Parrish a cease-and-desist letter, asserting that the Weekly

Cleanings Provision was unenforceable and a violation of the

 7
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

Fair Housing Act of 1968. The attorney alleged that Parrish

breached the rental agreement and committed fraud, and demanded

that Parrish: (1) stop enforcing the Weekly Cleaning Provision;

(2) reduce rent by fifty percent for September, October, and

November; (3) pay $5,000.00 in reasonable attorney’s fees; and

(4) pay $10,000.00 in general damages.

 That same day, Parrish rejected the demands and countered

that the request to simply not enforce the Weekly Cleanings

Provision was not reasonable. It suggested as an alternative

that the Fahns not be present in the property during the weekly

cleanings. Parrish indicated that it followed strict industry

protocols for its cleaning crew. It noted that all of employees

are screened daily, wear full personal equipment (including

masks and gloves), and use CDC-approved cleaning products. It

stated, “this is not a negotiation. Your clients have a binding

Lease. They will comply with the terms of that Lease or it will

be terminated.”

 On November 27, Parrish terminated the Fahns’ tenancy,

effective as of November 30 and filed a complaint for summary

possession on November 30.

 On December 31, the Fahns vacated the rental property.

Parrish retained $5,471.44 of the $6,000.00 security deposit to

clean, replace, and repair the property.

 8
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 2. HCRC Proceedings

 In December 2020, the Fahns filed a complaint with the

HCRC, alleging that Parrish “unlawfully discriminated against

[them] on the basis of disability by failing to engage in the

interactive process and by failing to provide a reasonable

accommodation for [Robert]’s disabilities.”

 Following an investigation, the HCRC “found that there was

reasonable cause to believe that unlawful discriminatory

practices had occurred.” When conciliation efforts proved

unsuccessful, the parties received notices of the right to sue

in March 2023. The Fahns exercised their right to sue in April

2023.

 3. Circuit Court Proceedings

 In July 2023, the H
